#9712. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9711. How Security Vendors Are Tackling Access-Control Challenges for AI Agents

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Identity, runtime and development controls are converging as enterprises are tasked with keeping agents within their assigned tasks. But vendors' approaches vary, so CISOs face a choice.

As organizations expand their use of artificial intelligence agents to perform tasks traditionally done by employees, security teams must control not only which systems agents can access, but which actions they are authorized to take.

The Blueprint Alliance, an industry group advocating for coordinated controls, notes that 92% of organizations use autonomous AI agents, but only 34% secure them with the same rigor as they do for human users.

Many vendors have begun adding capabilities to better control agents. Their approaches overlap, leaving CISOs to determine how the new offerings fit into a coherent security architecture that keeps agents focused on their assigned tasks and prevents overpermissioning machine identities beyond what their human users can access.

Earlier this month, CrowdStrike introduced what it calls an AI Kill Switch, which gives security teams a way to block an agent’s access to AI models via connected gateways. The new AI Kill Switch, launched during CrowdStrike's Fal.Con Europe conference in Barcelona this month, extends Falcon Guardian, the AI detection-and-response offering that supports Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints. Guardian discovers agents and controls which ones may run and connects prompts, identities, tool calls and skills to downstream actions in an execution graph.

Related:Phishing-Resistant Isn't Enough; Yubico Takes Aim at Identity-Verification Gap

The kill switch works with CrowdStrike's Falcon AI Gateway or connected third-party gateways. Its current enforcement point is model access, rather than every system an agent can reach. CrowdStrike says it will later extend the capability to terminate agent processes and revoke their access to enterprise resources.

"The hardest case is the agent that behaves abnormally without breaking a business process rule," CrowdStrike's chief product officer AJ Shipley said during an October 29 media roundtable discussion.

Discussing agent insider threat detection, Shipley described an approach that establishes a baseline of expected agent and user behavior and then detects deviations, even when no explicit policy violation occurs.

CrowdStrike also announced earlier this month agreements to acquire two startups — Fiddler AI and Dreadnode — extending its push into agent observability and pre-deployment security testing. Fiddler evaluates agents and helps explain their behavior in production, while Dreadnode tests models, applications and agents for security weaknesses before deployment. The Wall Street Journal reported a combined purchase price of approximately $495 million. The acquisitions have not yet closed.

Related:Cyera's Oasis Security Buy Is All About AI Agent Control

CrowdStrike is one of several vendors addressing agent access controls. Anaconda is combining agentic software development with autonomous security testing; Cisco and Teleport are tying access to infrastructure identity; Okta is enforcing identity policy when agents call tools; and Fortinet is extending controls over execution and application behavior.

Anaconda, for instance, is approaching the problem through application development by pairing agentic software development with autonomous security testing. Last month, it expanded its AI Dev Factory, combining development agent swarms with autonomous red-team agents that probe models, agents and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for weaknesses. The release incorporates technology from Anaconda's August acquisition of Enkrypt AI, supporting red teaming across more than 300 attack categories and runtime guardrails that approve, modify or block risky behavior.

Anaconda's earlier acquisitions of Outerbounds, Kilo Code and Enkrypt AI collectively bring together production orchestration, agentic development and AI security. “Our roadmap out for all three acquisitions would have been about two or three years’ worth of engineering effort,” Anaconda CEO David DeSanto says, describing Enkrypt as the final component needed to accomplish this goal.

Related:USA Fencing Lunges Into the Hidden Identity Challenge in Amateur Sports

Testing agents is one requirement; limiting their authority in production is another. Cisco is approaching that problem through infrastructure identity, becoming Teleport's largest strategic investor in August. Teleport's open-source platform replaces passwords and permanent SSH keys with ephemeral certificates.

Teleport CEO Ev Kontsevoy describes an incident in which a customer deployed an agent to process data and update a database. When the intended database became unavailable, the agent found another and tried to update it. The agent was trying to complete its assignment rather than respond to an attacker. Its improvisation nevertheless exposed the difference between granting access and containing behavior.

"Would you say it's a security accident or what? Whatever it is, it's terrifying when it happens, particularly at scale," Kontsevoy tells Dark Reading.

Cisco and Teleport's partnership addresses containment through verified infrastructure identities and access granted "just in time, just enough," says Peter Bailey, Cisco's senior VP and general manager for security. "We want to be able to take action and stop action based upon identity," Bailey says.

On October 26, Cisco introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, applying the partnership's infrastructure-identity approach to administrators and agents. Cisco says it provides temporary, identity-bound access to network infrastructure, records sessions and ends privileges when the task is complete.

Kontsevoy describes attaching privileges to tasks rather than permanently assigning them to accounts. A deployment ticket could identify the engineer, laptop and CI/CD pipeline involved. Each is granted necessary privileges, which disappear when the ticket closes. Teleport's MCP gateway also enforces policy and tracks relationships among initiating actors, agents and subagents, he says.

When an agent acts on an employee's behalf, controls must distinguish the agent's permissions from those of the person directing the agent to avoid inappropriate privilege escalation.

Consider a scenario in which an HR assistant runs on a service account that can read every employee record. A contractor asking the agent for the CEO's compensation could get the response since the assistant has access the contractor doesn't. According to Okta, this agent would be a "confused deputy," as it exercises authority the requester lacks.

To address this scenario, Okta's Agent Gateway treats agents as "first-class" identities; it preserves the distinction between their permissions and those of the users directing them. It requires a credential that identifies both the user and the agent and uses token exchange to preserve the delegation context. The gateway limits the tools available, while the downstream MCP server enforces the user's record-level access. Agent Gateway is now generally available as an addition to AI agents, an identity-security offering made generally available in April.

In an October 8 blog post, Okta described plans for Cross App Access support and a gateway-based kill switch. Officials said the latter "will make agent deactivation immediate, down to tokens already issued, by rejecting any request carrying a token issued to a deactivated agent."

Okta is not alone in extending identity controls to agents. At its Fal.Con conference in Las Vegas in September, CrowdStrike also announced Agentic Identity Provider, designed to establish trusted agent identities, broker time-limited access and link actions to initiating employees or systems.

Microsoft is pursuing a related approach through Project Perception, connecting agent identity, behavioral risk signals and access controls across its security products via its new Guardian Agent capabilities

Meanwhile, Fortinet is extending AI inspection across its existing network security products. Last month, the company announced the FortiGuard Inline AI Security Service for FortiGate customers and described expanded FortiAIGate capabilities incorporating Virtue AI technology, which Fortinet acquired earlier this year. Virtue AI adds policy-derived guardrails, continuous assessment, code analysis and agent red teaming. Fortinet executive vice president Anthony James describes more than 50 simulated application environments in which customers can test agent boundaries before connecting to real systems. James says Virtue can block an agent from communicating with MCP tools or servers not approved for its task and detect prompt sequences that progress from innocuous to malicious.

James says FortiAIGate began by monitoring communications to and from AI infrastructure. Customers deploying agents sought a deeper understanding of the application. Models, MCP servers, agents and skills “require a little deeper application knowledge than just interpreting the network traffic,” James says.

Overlapping approaches have prompted coordination efforts. In September, Okta announced the Blueprint Alliance with vendors including AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow and Zscaler. The group aims to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors’ products.

The alliance has outlined principles for agent identity, task-scoped access, monitoring and containment. Whether those principles translate into interoperable products and expanded adoption remains to be seen.

Taken together, these approaches point to a common requirement: keeping an agent’s access tied to its assigned task. Identity verification, security testing and runtime monitoring address different parts of that requirement, but no single control confirms that an agent will remain within its assignment.

Emerging control planes aim to connect those controls across tools and systems—limiting agents to their assigned tasks rather than letting AI software determine how far its authority extends.

Jeffrey Schwartz is a New York–based freelance writer specializing in information security and enterprise IT. Focused on the constant pace of technological change, Jeff has covered the evolution of technologies, including professional broadcast, computing, networking, the Internet, mobile communications, modern cloud infrastructure and software development for over 30 years.

Jeff has contributed to Dark Reading since 2022 and has written for Channel Futures for over five years. Before launching his freelance career, he was an editor at 1105 Media, where he served as editor-in-chief of Redmond magazine and contributed to its sister publications, including Redmond Channel Partner, Application Development Trends, and Virtualization Review.

Previously, Jeff held editorial roles at CMP Media’s CommunicationsWeek, InternetWeek, and VARBusiness. Earlier contributions include Pro Sound News, Television Broadcast, Videography, Sound & Communications, Post magazine and Crain’s Electronic Media. Jeff holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in Communications and Journalism from Adelphi University. More details are available on Jeff’s LinkedIn profile: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeffaschwartz.

#9709. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

The FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently shows that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

The golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

The biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:

A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you plan intentionally from the start.

Before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

There is no single right number, but the median US wedding cost of $10,000 to $15,000 is achievable for most couples without going into debt. Focus on what matters most to you and cut everything else. A $10,000 wedding with great food, a good photographer, and people you love is better than a $30,000 wedding that starts your marriage with financial stress.

No. Wedding debt is one of the worst forms of consumer debt because it funds a single day with no residual asset value. The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

Any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. Budget based on what you can afford independently, then treat any parental contribution as a bonus.

Yes. Friday and Sunday weddings typically cost 20-30% less than Saturday weddings for the same venue and vendors. Some venues offer discounts of 40% or more for weekday weddings (Monday through Thursday). Off-season months like January, February, March, and November also offer significant savings.

Tips for vendors (plan 15-20% for catering staff, bartenders, and drivers), alterations for wedding attire ($200-$500), marriage license fees ($30-$100), and overtime charges if the reception runs past the contracted time. Build a 10% contingency buffer into your total budget for these surprises.

Set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion. If family members want upgrades, they are welcome to fund those specific additions. Protect your financial foundation — the marriage matters more than the wedding, and starting debt-free sets up your partnership for success.

A meaningful wedding does not require $30,000 or any specific dollar amount. Set a cash budget based on what you can afford without debt, allocate spending toward what creates lasting memories (food, photography, people), and cut everything else. Every dollar you save on the wedding is a dollar that starts compounding toward your financial independence. The couples with the strongest financial futures are the ones who celebrate joyfully within their means and invest the difference.

#9707. Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites

At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

This entry was posted on Tuesday 17th of November 2026 09:52 PM

Using an A/B testing platform as the delivery mechanism is a genuinely uncomfortable escalation: the tool that decides which visitors see which experience was never modeled as a malware distribution channel, so none of the usual detections fire. The operational discipline angle is what stands out – attackers versioning and measuring payloads like product features means defenders need the same rigor about what their third-party tags are allowed to change. Supply-chain reviews for marketing stacks rarely get the scrutiny payments or auth integrations do; this will change that.

But this is where we are: the Web, which was intended to let users share information, and for the sharee to display it in any way *they* want to see it in, to now, when it’s a marketing platform, with mis-targeted marketing, and almost nothing that’s not trying to sell you something.

I look forward to ’29, with a Democratic administration, and QUALIFIED Cabinet members, so I can, for example, report all the false medical advice ads on youtube. (sorry, there is, in fact, diabetes in Israel, etc, etc.)

CSP is still a bit flawed, but is probably the best defense we have against XSS (cross-site script injections). However, having CSP rules in place, would not have prevented this at all since this was a supply chain attack on a trusted provider. Even if they hosted the 3rd party scripts themselves, the downloaded script would have contained the malware. Once that’s running, game is over…. they’d just make simple requests to the malicious domain with the stolen information. The end-user would need to have something in place that prevented the outgoing traffic. Making this situation worse, is that many sites (due to incompetence) will put in CORS rules that effectively wildcard allowed origins. (a different attack, but one where you’d be able to make cross-site requests from a scam site with the user’s credentials) Unfortunately, AI supplies a lot of people with code that has these vulnerabilities already baked in… garbage in, garbage out…

My understanding is that this attack directed the JavaScript to download malware from several domains that were definitely not Optimizely domains, and very much would be caught by a competently implemented CSP.

CSP headers would have stopped that attack, but only if using Optimizely didn’t already require setting ‘strict-dynamic’, which requires nonces/hashes instead (those aren’t really foolproof… once they are able to inject a script they can steal those too) But let’s say the CSP headers stopped the attack, the attackers could still fallback to the initial injected code. The attacker would only lose the ability to dynamically update things. (it’d force them to update from the already compromised supplier…)

The problem is these sites uses those stupid content delivery networks and if you block them then you do not get the body of the site. As a security person this leads to a problem when trying to provide access for people in your organization. How can I provide you access to a site where i know these cdns are in place but you have to have it in order to do your job?

The line that stuck with me was Scott Helme’s point that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy — a site can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code being at fault. That is exactly why I have become sceptical of keeping my most sensitive secrets inside the browser at all, even in a well-regarded password manager. If a trusted script can be swapped for a malicious one, the safest place for a seed phrase or a master password is somewhere no web page, extension or third-party script can reach. That thinking is why, as the developer of GhostCore, I built it as a fully offline iOS vault for seed phrases, passwords, cards and offline 2FA, with no cloud sync and no network access for the vault itself. CSPs and script blockers help a lot, as this article shows, but for the credentials that would be catastrophic to lose, removing them from the browser entirely feels like the more durable fix.

And it will be specifically targeted when it becomes used by N% of possibly money-having users. Are you actually advertising here?

This is precisely why several requirements were added to the PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) v 4.0 to make developers and deployers of payment pages inventory and authorize all the scripts that appear on the page, plus prevention of executing any authorized scripts. If payment card data was stolen, those authorizations are not occurring. PCI DSS Compliance is at risk for any of the sites that are not tracking this adequately. I’d strongly advise QSAs to investigate even more thoroughly exactly how this supply chain is monitiored and controlled.

And since EVERY PIC Compliant site now knows that this is a possibility, if I were still a QSA, I’d be asking in the next assessment for evidence of the Incident Response plan having been activated to ensure that no such breach had occurred on my assessed entity’s site, or the steps taken by the site to further stengthen their solution. IMHO there is no excuse for not having initiated an IRP by now.

#9705. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

#9704. CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9703. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9701. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9699. Every Forward-Deployed Engineer Is a Bug Report About Your Infrastructure

Data Scientist and a PhD candidate in Information Technology, where I examine IT flexibility & AI adoption.

Data Scientist and a PhD candidate in Information Technology, where I examine IT flexibility & AI adoption.

Data Scientist and a PhD candidate in Information Technology, where I examine IT flexibility & AI adoption.

A few years ago, the only people I knew with "forward-deployed engineer" in their title worked at Palantir. This year it feels like every AI company is hiring them, and a growing number of the companies buying AI are too.

The numbers are hard to ignore. LinkedIn reported that forward-deployed engineering positions grew 42-fold between 2023 and 2025. LinkUp, which tracks job listings, counted about 300 open FDE roles through 2022 and 2023, and more than 5,000 by early 2026. An executive search firm told TechCrunch that the share of companies planning to hire FDEs went from 5–10% at the start of this year to 70% by the end of June.

Most of what I've read about this treats it as a career story. Good pay, new title, here's how to land the job. That's fine, but the more interesting question to me is why a role grows that fast in the first place. My answer: companies are hiring people to supply the flexibility their systems don't have.

CIEL HR, which analyzed FDE hiring this summer, describes the job as integrating AI into existing technology environments and connecting models with business workflows. (If you want the basics on the role itself, Paolo Perrone has a solid explainer on HackerNoon already.)

That description is accurate. It's also a polite way of saying most of the work is plumbing and translation. Figuring out which of six systems actually owns the customer record. Writing glue code so a nightly batch export from 2011 can feed a model. Sitting with the ops team until you learn the three exception rules nobody ever wrote down. Very little of it touches the model.

I study IT infrastructure flexibility, and this is the part that clicked for me. Back in 1995, Nancy Duncan described flexible infrastructure in terms of three technical properties: connectivity, compatibility, and modularity. Can the pieces reach each other? Can they share data that means the same thing on both sides? Can you swap one out without breaking the rest?

In 2000, Terry Anthony Byrd and Douglas Turner added a fourth: IT personnel flexibility. Their argument was that infrastructure includes people, and specifically how well those people understand both the technology and the business around it. A company with rigid systems and adaptable staff still has flexibility. It just keeps it in people's heads instead of in the architecture.

What I find telling is a follow-up Byrd and Turner published in 2001. They surveyed CIOs, mostly at Fortune 2000 companies, and found technical skills mattered most for infrastructure flexibility. Business knowledge, interpersonal skills and technology management didn't show the positive relationships they expected.

Now go read an FDE job posting. Yes, it wants a strong engineer. It also wants someone who will embed with the customer, learn their workflow, manage stakeholders and translate between engineers and the business. Those are the skills CIOs rated low 25 years ago, and the market now pays a premium for them. I don't think AI made those skills important. I think it showed how much enterprise systems had been quietly leaning on them all along.

When systems can't connect, can't agree on what the data means, or can't change without breaking, somebody fills the gap by hand. An FDE is a very good somebody. In the short term that's often the fastest route to a working deployment, and I'm not knocking it.

But a person standing in for an interface behaves differently from an interface.

For one, it doesn't get reused. A clean API built for your first AI use case is still there for the fifth. A workaround that lives in one engineer's head only helps the next project if that engineer gets assigned to it.

It also leaves. If the FDE works for a vendor, what they learned about how your systems really fit together walks out when the contract ends. TechCrunch reported that some enterprises are now building internal FDE teams instead of relying on outside firms, partly to keep proprietary processes away from AI vendors. So at least some companies have noticed.

And it hides the cost. The pilot works, so the infrastructure gap never turns into a budget line. The next team pays for the same integration all over again.

Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise survey points the same way. Among more than 3,200 leaders, insufficient worker skills came out as the biggest barrier to integrating AI. Yet 84% of organizations hadn't redesigned jobs or workflows around it. Plenty of companies feel the people gap. Far fewer are changing how their people and systems fit together.

Hire FDEs if you need them. Early in a deployment, someone who's comfortable working in the mess is worth a lot. The real question is what you keep after they're done.

Start by asking them to write down every workaround: each manual mapping, one-off script, and undocumented rule they had to rely on. That list is the most honest map of your infrastructure gaps you'll ever get, and you've already paid for it.

Then watch for reuse. When your second and third AI projects kick off, check how much of the first project's integration work they could pick up. If the answer is close to none, you're paying for human middleware every single time.

If the FDEs are external, pair each with an internal counterpart, and ensure the code and documentation end up in your repositories rather than the vendor's.

Look inside, too. Your data engineers, analysts, and data scientists who already know the business domain are some of the cheapest FDEs you'll find. Give them time for integration work and credit for it, not just for shipping models.

Finally, take the workarounds that keep showing up and fund the boring fixes: real interfaces, shared data definitions, services you can change on their own. That's how flexibility moves out of people's heads and into the architecture.

That's the fair pushback. AI is new, the interfaces aren't standard yet, and someone has to bridge the gap for now. For a first deployment, I agree. Even the people recruiting FDEs don't describe the role as permanent: the search firm founder TechCrunch spoke with said the job could disappear within 5 to 10 years. (His firm places FDEs, so read his numbers with that in mind.)

If the role is temporary, though, what it teaches you about your systems shouldn't be.

I've started thinking of every FDE hire as a bug report about the infrastructure. It tells you exactly where your systems can't absorb something new on their own. You can keep renting that flexibility one engagement at a time. Or you can take what those engineers learn and build it in, so the next project needs fewer of them.

Data Scientist and a PhD candidate in Information Technology, where I examine IT flexibility & AI adoption.
