#9684. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.

If you’re on Linux or you want to serve the model from the CLI, you can run the following command for the fixed-loop model:

To run the variable-loop model, you can run

To load the 8-bit weights, change the suffix to :Q8_0.

Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

#9682. Running 10x Faster in the Wrong Direction: The AI Productivity Paradox

Your team adopted AI tools. PRs are flowing, prototypes appear overnight, and the roadmap deck looks fantastic. So why are customer metrics flat? Let's talk about it.

In July 2026, Marty Cagan wrote about the AI productivity paradox. Teams are clearly delivering faster, but outcomes are not improving. He cites McKinsey on growing adoption with a hard-to-find performance impact, and an Atlassian report where most executives say AI sped things up but very few can show a return across the whole organization.

It is not really a paradox. Most people point AI at the old project-model way of working, and slowness was never the only problem there. That model was built to deliver output, not outcomes. Hilary Gridley said it has never been easier to run 10 times faster in the wrong direction. Ouch, and accurate.

Weak teams use AI to churn out business cases, roadmaps, PRDs and code faster. Strong teams use it to find something worth building.

If you nodded at two or more, keep reading.

Monday: pick one assumption and write an experiment card with a success threshold. Tuesday: build a clickable prototype with AI tools. Wednesday: test with five customers. Thursday: compare the evidence to the threshold, then decide to build to earn, iterate or stop. Friday: record the learning and update your bets. The point is to keep discovery honest and disposable.

Assumption we are testing. Which risk: value, usability, feasibility or viability. What we built and with which tools. Who we test with and how. Success threshold agreed before the test. Result. Decision. And my favorite line: what this prototype is NOT, which is production code or a customer commitment.

Teresa Torres of Product Talk describes evals as a discovery habit. Define what good looks like, test outputs systematically, and track quality over time, including after any prompt, model or data change.

Name a human owner for every AI-assisted decision that reaches customers, keep prototype data away from production, and keep customer data out of tools that security has not approved.

Pick one team, give it an outcome with a baseline, and ask it to use AI for experiments instead of extra output. At the end, check whether AI shortened the time to a decision or just grew the pile of artifacts.

Full guide with the gate checklist and templates: https://productleadersdayindia.org/blogs/ai-driven-product-operating-model/product-operating-model-in-the-ai-era.html

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:

What these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most important distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution plan balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data shows that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($25,500 in 2027), HSA ($4,500 individual / $9,000 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

Fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $25,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

The average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

At 7% average returns, that alone grows to over $950,000 in 15 years — before counting the $50,000 you already have. Starting late is not ideal, but a high savings rate compresses the timeline dramatically.

Add up every 401(k), IRA, Roth IRA, HSA, and other retirement account balance. Include employer-sponsored plans from previous jobs — many people have orphaned 401(k) accounts they have forgotten about. Exclude your home equity and Social Security for now.

Most employers allow you to change your 401(k) contribution rate at any time. Increasing by 2% of salary is small enough that you will barely notice the paycheck reduction, but it compounds dramatically over time. Repeat this increase every six months until you are maxing out your 401(k).

Roughly one in four employees leaves free employer match money on the table. If your employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary, you need to contribute at least 6% to capture the full match. This is an instant 50% return on your money — no investment can beat it.

A Roth IRA provides tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement, with no required minimum distributions. The 2026 limit is $7,000 ($8,000 if 50+). If your income exceeds the Roth limits, use the backdoor Roth conversion strategy to contribute indirectly.

Fidelity recommends having 1x your annual salary saved by age 30. For someone earning $55,000, that means $55,000 in retirement accounts. The FI community targets higher — $50,000 to $100,000 by 30 is common among aggressive savers. The national median for under-35 is only $13,000, so if you have more than that, you are already ahead of most peers.

The average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

Generally no. While your home is part of your net worth, it is not liquid retirement savings you can draw from to cover living expenses. You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

It is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $75,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement plan; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

#9680. The Benefits and Risks of Updating Multiple Programs Through a Shared Handler

Founder and chief engineer at Extella (https://extella.dev). Named inventor on U.S. patents in computing architecture.

Founder and chief engineer at Extella (https://extella.dev). Named inventor on U.S. patents in computing architecture.

Founder and chief engineer at Extella (https://extella.dev). Named inventor on U.S. patents in computing architecture.

For developers maintaining internal tools: changing shared rules in reports and calculations, checking the results, and restoring previous behavior.

We updated one shared handler in Extella and changed the formatting and validation rules of 40 report programs on their next run, without modifying their source code. When we deliberately introduced an error, a validation check detected incorrect totals in 35 of the reports and blocked the update. After we bypassed the check to test recovery, restoring the previous handler brought all 40 reports back to their correct totals.

The approach puts shared logic in a handler: code that executes commands written in a small language for a particular task. Each program describes what needs to be done, while the handler takes care of execution. Libraries and services also let programs share logic; here we examine what this arrangement requires in practice.

The experiment showed both sides of shared execution: one update can change multiple programs at once, but one error can affect many of them.

For a developer maintaining these programs, the next question is how to test a shared change and restore the previous behavior if it goes wrong. We follow those steps below, then examine a separate experiment in which an AI model uses prepared commands to write new programs.

Changing shared rules separately from a report requires separating two parts of the program. The report description holds data and commands. The handler holds the calculation, formatting, and validation code. A small language with commands for a particular set of tasks is called a domain-specific language, or DSL.

The first handler needs to be written and tested against examples with known results. The developer also defines which commands it supports and what each one means. If those commands cover a new report’s requirements, its author can specify the data and commands using the calculation and validation code already in the handler.

A familiar analogy is a template engine: a template specifies fields and placeholders, and the engine turns them into a finished page. Here, too, the report description is separate from the code that executes it. Changing the shared formatting code changes how reports look on subsequent runs (Scheme 1).

It performs shared calculations, validation, and formatting. After an update, programs apply the new rules on subsequent runs without source changes, provided the handler remains compatible with the existing commands.

A short example shows exactly what stays in a program when its handler changes. In the ledger language, add N adds a number to the total and sub N subtracts one. A Python handler was tested with four saved programs. One looked like this:

Starting at zero, the handler calculates 5 + 7 − 2 = 10. The first version returned the total; the second added the number of commands and the largest number specified. The total calculation stayed the same.

After the handler was replaced, all four programs returned their previous totals with new response fields. Their source text was neither changed nor saved again.

This is backward-compatible for an application that reads only the total field. A strict check of the field set could reject the new response. That would require preserving the old format or updating dependent programs.

At this point, a developer might ask why a custom language is needed when shared code can already live in a function, library, or service. A Python function is indeed enough for two arithmetic commands. Ledger shows how to separate a program from its execution; this example establishes no advantage over an ordinary function.

In our comparisons, an ordinary script called programs through MCP (Model Context Protocol), an interface for connecting tools. MCP provided the call interface; no AI model chose the actions. A simple MCP server could also store and run programs. Windmill, a script-running environment, provided version history and rollback; it was tested on one machine.

The next test therefore follows a shared change through a set of reports: applying it, detecting a defect, and restoring the previous results. That requires an expected total for each report.

The main experiment used 40 small report programs containing different sets of amounts. The shared handler was updated to format totals and reject duplicate row names. All 40 programs used the new rules on subsequent runs without source changes. The developer could maintain these rules in one place while each report kept its own data and commands. The next step was to check the results across all 40 reports.

We then tested what would happen if the shared update were wrong. A deliberately faulty version dropped the fractional part of each row's amount before adding the amounts together. Before installing it, a separate validation program compared the results with values calculated in advance. It found 35 incorrect totals out of 40 and rejected the update. The previous handler remained in place and continued to produce 40 correct totals.

Directly registering the handler could bypass this check. The experiment did exactly that: it installed the faulty version, obtained incorrect totals, then restored the previous version and recovered all 40 correct results.

The check worked because correct totals were already known for all 40 programs. Recovery used a saved copy of the previous handler, registered again after the faulty update.

The 40-report experiment tested updating and recovery; it did not compare maintenance costs with a library or service. A separate test changed the appearance of one report and showed no time or token savings. Each approach was tried once.

Checking totals is not enough when reports run on different devices. The new handler also has to run in each environment. Each device needs a runner, the appropriate handler version, and the dependencies it uses. Before updating, check the environment and run validation programs on each device. Saving the new source code alone does not establish that these requirements are met.

A separate experiment examines dependencies and code delivery on two devices. It updated a saved calculation operation while leaving the language handlers unchanged. It helps explain deployment requirements, but does not test replacing a shared handler.

So far, we have examined changes to programs that already work. The prepared handler can also serve the next program: a person or an AI model describes the task using its commands. The model can draw on operations whose execution and checks have already been implemented. To find out whether such commands help a model, we ran a separate employee-scheduling experiment comparing schedule correctness and token use.

The model wrote either a Python program that produced a schedule or commands in a scheduling language. Prewritten code checked hours and constraints, such as whether enough employees were available at a given time. Both formats used the same rules; in the DSL version, the checks were part of the handler and made no AI calls.

Three approaches were compared on six tasks using qwen-flash. Each task was repeated three times for each approach, giving 18 task runs per approach. In the approaches with feedback, a run allowed up to three attempts: after an error, the model received feedback and could revise its program.

In the last two approaches, the model received the same general rules and up to three attempts. Python with revisions used about 5.7 times as many tokens as the scheduling DSL. These totals include both successful and unsuccessful task runs. Eight DSL runs still failed validation. In two cases, Python with revisions passed while the scheduling DSL failed.

With the stronger qwen3.7-max-2026-06-08 model, each task was run once per approach. All three approaches passed all six tasks, and the scheduling DSL had no token advantage. These results come from saved logs. The logs do not include the models' final programs, so they cannot be used to independently rerun every generated schedule.

These results concern a model using commands that are already available. The token totals exclude developing and testing the handler. They compare the scheduling approach as a whole, including the language, execution, and feedback. They do not measure the cost of updating reports. A stronger model could help write a handler for a smaller model to use, but the experiment did not measure the full cost of that workflow.

The report experiment checked totals, while the scheduling experiment checked constraints. A working system also needs compatibility with applications that consume the programs' output. A breaking change to that output requires preserving the previous format or updating dependent applications.

Recovery needs a saved working handler and a way to restore it even if the new version is broken. Restoring the code does not undo completed actions, such as an email already sent. Built-in version history and updates during running calls were not tested.

The checking code can also be wrong. The first schedule validator missed a five-minute gap; this article uses the corrected experiment. The checks therefore need tests with valid and invalid inputs. Changes to the checking code, including changes made by an agent, need review separately from changes to the program being checked.

The execution path can add latency. A separate comparison made 30 repeated calls per method. The medians were about 9.4 seconds through the program-execution service and 0.025 seconds through a simple local runner. Computation ran on the same laptop, but the call paths differed; this does not isolate the cost of the language itself.

Checks in the handler help find errors in a program, but do not restrict the handler’s own permissions. In the configuration described here, the handler runs with the user’s permissions, so access to files, the network, and system commands needs separate restrictions.

A handler is worth considering when several tasks use a stable set of operations. Reports may contain different data while calculating and displaying totals according to shared rules. A new report can then use existing commands. When a shared rule changes, the developer updates the handler and checks every affected report.

The initial preparation falls to whoever first defines the commands, writes the handler, and tests it. Other people and AI models can then compose programs from those operations, reusing the code that executes and checks them. The developer still needs to check that each program meets its requirements. A task outside the supported operations requires extending the handler and testing it again.

A library or service also supports shared code. The choice depends on how well a separate language expresses your tasks and whether reuse justifies maintaining it. Compare the full cycle: building the handler, adding programs, changing shared rules, checking results, and recovering from errors. For one report, this extra work may be unnecessary.

We ran these experiments, calling this mechanism CSPL (Container Specific Programming Language): each saved program specifies its language, and a handler registered on the device executes its commands. The code, Erun logs, and results of the 40-report and scheduling experiments are available on GitHub.

To assess the approach for your own tools, choose a small set of programs that share rules. Establish their expected results, change one rule, and check whether you can both apply and reverse the change. Account for writing the handler and maintaining those checks before deciding whether a custom language is worth keeping.

#9679. Oracle AI Database 26ai(23.26.4):BAR_CHART - A New Way to Visualize Data

Oracle introduces the BAR_CHART SQL function to make query results easier to read and understand. This function converts numeric or Boolean values into visual bars using characters.

The function uses a value to determine the length of a bar. You can also customize its scale, width, and display character. The general syntax is: BAR_CHART(value, maximum, minimum, width, symbol) The function accepts five arguments: value: The numeric or Boolean value to display as a bar.  maximum: The upper limit of the scale. Default: 100 for numeric values and 1 for Boolean values. minimum: The lower limit of the scale. Default: 0. width: The maximum bar length in characters. Default: 10 for numeric values and 1 for Boolean values. symbol: The character used to draw the bar.

One practical use of this function is monitoring tablespace utilization. For example:

In this example, BAR_CHART displays tablespace utilization as a visual bar. A tablespace with higher usage gets a longer bar, making it easier to identify tablespaces that are running out of space. Customizing the Bar You can customize the appearance of the bar by specifying its width and symbol. For example:

Here: 100 defines the maximum value. 0 defines the minimum value. 20 sets the bar width to 20 characters. '#' specifies the character used to draw the bar.

You can also use a CASE expression to select different symbols based on a condition:

This allows you to represent different utilization levels with different characters.

Another useful capability is combining multiple BAR_CHART results using the concatenation operator (||).

This example creates a bar with three different sections, each representing a specific range of tablespace utilization. The first section represents values from 0 to 70, the second from 70 to 85, and the third from 85 to 100.

#9678. Ginger VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?


Ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market. This article aims to highlight the specifics of each one so that you can make a more informed decision about the one you'll use.

What is Grammarly?

If you are a writer, you must have heard of  Grammarly before. Grammarly has over 10M users across the globe, it's probably the most popular AI writing enhancement tool, without a doubt. That's why there's a high chance that you already know about Grammarly.

But today we are going to do a comparison between Ginger and Grammarly, So let's define Grammarly here. Like Ginger, Grammarly is an AI writing assistant that checks for grammatical errors, spellings, and punctuation. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

While the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

Features of Grammarly

  • Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a personal dictionary 
  • Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Understand inconsistencies. 
  • Detect unclear structure. 
  • Detect Plagiarism.
  • Explore overuse of words and wordiness. 
  • Get to know about the improper tones. 
  • Discover the insensitive language aligns with your intent, audience, style, emotion, and more.


What is Ginger

 Ginger is a writing enhancement tool that not only catches typos and grammatical mistakes but also suggests content improvements. As you type, it picks up on errors then shows you what’s wrong, and suggests a fix. It also provides you with synonyms and definitions of words and allows you to translate your text into dozens of languages.


Ginger Software: Features & Benefits

  • Ginger's software helps you identify and correct common grammatical mistakes, such as consecutive nouns, or contextual spelling correction.
  • The sentence rephrasing feature can help you convey your meaning perfectly.
  • Ginger acts like a personal coach that helps you practice certain exercises based on your mistakes.
  • The dictionary feature helps users understand the meanings of words.

In addition, the program provides a text reader, so you can gauge your writing’s conversational tone.


Ginger vs Grammarly

Grammarly and Ginger are two popular grammar checker software brands that help you to become a better writer. But if you’re undecided about which software to use, consider these differences:

  • Grammarly only supports the English language while Ginger supports 40+ languages.
  • Grammarly offers a wordiness feature while Ginger lacks a Wordiness feature.
  • Grammarly shows an accuracy score while Ginger lacks an accuracy score feature.
  • Grammarly has a plagiarism checker while ginger doesn't have such a feature.
  • Grammarly can recognize an incorrect use of numbers while Ginger can’t recognize an incorrect use of numbers.
  • Grammarly and Ginger both have mobile apps.
  • Ginger and Grammarly offer monthly, quarterly, and annual plans.
  • Grammarly allows you to check uploaded documents. while Ginger doesn't check uploaded documents.
  • Grammarly Offers a tone suggestion feature while Ginger doesn't offer a tone suggestion feature.
  • Ginger helps to translate documents into 40+ languages while Grammarly doesn't have a translation feature.
  • Ginger Offers text to speech features while Grammarly doesn't have such features.

  • On the other hand,  Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly, and $12/month for an annual subscription.

For companies with three or more employees, the Business plan costs $12.50/month for each member of your team. 

Ginger Wins Here

Ginger vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons


Grammarly Pros

  • Offers  free version
  • All-in-one tool (grammar checker + spell checker + punctuation checker)

Grammarly Cons

#9677. How to Install Claude Code on Android With Termux

AI coding agents are no longer limited to desktop computers.

With the right setup, you can run tools such as Claude Code directly on an Android phone using Termux. You do not need root access, a PC, or an Android emulator. This guide will show you how to set up Claude Code on Termux, explain two different installation paths, and cover some of the problems you may run into along the way.

The recommended approach uses Ubuntu inside Termux with proot-distro. It takes more storage than a native installation, but it gives the coding agent a more familiar Linux environment.

An AI coding agent is more than a chatbot that gives you code snippets.

A coding agent can work with files on your device, inspect an existing project, modify code, run commands, and help troubleshoot problems.

you can give the agent an existing project and ask it to inspect the code, make the required changes, and test the result.

Claude Code is one example of this type of tool. There are also other CLI-based coding agents that can be used from a Linux terminal.

On Android, Termux provides the terminal environment that makes this possible.

Before starting, check a few things first.

Your Android operating system needs to run on aarch64.

This is important because having a 64-bit ARM processor does not always mean that Android itself is running as a 64-bit operating system.

Some older or budget Android phones, including certain Samsung A-series devices, have shipped with a 32-bit Android OS even though their hardware is capable of 64-bit operation.

If uname -m returns something such as armv7l, this setup will not work as described here.

Install Termux from a current supported source such.

The Google Play situation has changed over time, but the Play Store build and the main Termux project have been separate, so using the established F-Droid/GitHub sources avoids mixing incompatible builds and packages.

You will need access to Claude if you are using Claude Code directly.

Authentication normally happens when you first start Claude Code.

The native route uses considerably less storage.

The Ubuntu route is heavier. Keep roughly 2 GB or more of free space available so the container and its packages have room to install properly.

There are two practical approaches worth knowing about.

The first approach runs the Linux ARM64 Claude Code binary directly through a compatibility layer in Termux.

It is attractive because the installation is smaller and you do not need an Ubuntu container.

However, this is not official Android support. Claude Code is distributed as a Linux binary, while Android uses the Bionic C library rather than the glibc environment expected by that binary.

Current community installers work around this by using tools such as glibc-runner and patching the binary's Linux interpreter.

There has also been a period where newer Claude Code releases broke older native Termux installation methods because the package moved to platform-specific native binaries.

Older guides often solved this by pinning Claude Code to version 2.1.112. Newer compatibility workarounds now exist, but the important point is that native Termux support is still a compatibility solution rather than an official Android build.

So if you see an older guide telling you to pin the Claude Code version, that advice comes from a real compatibility problem. It is not necessarily the only solution anymore.

The second approach places Ubuntu inside Termux.

proot-distro provides a Linux userland without requiring root access or a separate virtual machine.

This is the approach recommended in this guide.

The main advantage is that Claude Code sees a normal Linux environment instead of trying to operate directly against Android's userland.

It also gives you a useful Linux environment for other development tools.

There is a third option as well: Android Virtualization Framework (AVF) can provide a real Linux virtual machine on some newer devices. Current community documentation lists Pixel 6-class and newer supported devices as an experimental route. That setup is outside the scope of this guide.

proot-distro is what we will use to install and enter Ubuntu without root access.

Once the installation finishes, enter Ubuntu:

Your prompt should change to something similar to:

You are now inside the Ubuntu environment.

Your Ubuntu filesystem remains available between sessions.

Inside Ubuntu, update the package lists and installed packages:

This is worth doing before installing Claude Code because a fresh Ubuntu container may not have the latest packages and certificates required for downloads.

Current Claude Code documentation provides an official installer for Linux:

Anthropic's current documentation also supports an npm installation for Linux systems with Node.js, but the native installer is the simpler route here.

If the installer tells you that claude cannot be found, add its directory to your PATH:

If everything is working, you should get the installed Claude Code version. A common mistake here is trying to run claude immediately from a non-interactive shell before .bashrc has been loaded.

or starting a normal login shell solves that in most cases.

The first launch will ask you to authenticate. Depending on your Android version and browser setup, the authentication page may open automatically. On some older Android versions, you may need to copy the URL shown in the terminal and open it manually. Once authentication is complete, Claude Code can work with the files in your current project directory.

Suppose you have a Python project in your Ubuntu home directory.

From there, you can ask it to inspect the project, create files, explain existing code, or make changes.

The important difference from a normal AI chat is that the agent can work with the project itself rather than only seeing the code you manually paste into a conversation.

The setup is fairly straightforward, but Termux and Android introduce a few things that can be confusing.

One problem reported with native Termux installations involves DNS resolution. Android does not provide the normal Linux /etc/resolv.conf environment that many Linux programs expect. Some Linux binaries rely on a DNS resolver that reads this file, and when it is missing, they can fall back to a resolver address where nothing is listening.

This can result in connection attempts hanging or timing out. This is another reason the Ubuntu route is useful. If you encounter this problem on a native installation, check the documentation for the specific Termux/Claude compatibility layer you installed rather than randomly changing DNS settings.

Some current native installers include their own DNS workaround for affected devices.

If Claude installed successfully but the command cannot be found, check your PATH:

If you are using the native Termux route and Claude suddenly stops working after an update, check the version and the installation method you are using.

This has happened because Claude Code changed its binary distribution and older Termux workarounds were no longer compatible with newer releases.

If you want the least amount of troubleshooting, the Ubuntu route avoids much of this native Android compatibility layer.

Once everything is installed, you do not need to repeat the setup.

If you want to continue an existing Claude Code session, use the session commands supported by your installed Claude Code version.

If you are using a local routing proxy or another service outside Ubuntu, you may instead use two Termux sessions: one session keeps the routing service running while the other enters Ubuntu and runs Claude Code. For direct Claude API access, you can keep things much simpler and use a single Ubuntu session.

There is another setup that some Termux users experiment with.

A local AI router can sit between Claude Code and the model provider:

If a routing method depends on a provider's free tier or a third-party proxy, check the provider's current terms before relying on it.

Running an AI coding agent on a phone is useful, but a phone is still a phone.

AI coding agents can run commands, inspect files, and perform repeated operations.

Long sessions can therefore consume battery and generate heat, especially on less powerful phones.

Some Android manufacturers are aggressive about stopping background applications.

If you leave a long-running process in Termux and switch to another application, Android may eventually terminate it.

Battery optimization settings can also affect Termux.

proot-distro does not give you actual root privileges.

It creates a Linux-like environment in userspace. That is enough for many development tasks, but it does not provide the same control as a rooted Android device or a real Linux machine.

Termux, Android, Linux packages, and AI coding tools are all changing.

An update can occasionally introduce compatibility problems.

This is especially important with native Termux installations because they depend on compatibility layers between Android and Linux binaries.

The Ubuntu approach reduces some of those problems, but it does not eliminate them completely.

You do not need a PC to experiment with AI coding agents anymore. With Termux and proot-distro, an Android phone can provide a surprisingly capable Linux development environment.

For the setup covered here, Ubuntu inside Termux is the route to start with. It gives Claude Code a conventional Linux environment and avoids many of the compatibility problems that can appear when trying to run Linux binaries directly against Android.

The native Termux approach is still interesting if you want a smaller setup and are comfortable dealing with compatibility workarounds.

But whichever route you choose, the basic idea is simple:

Once that is working, your phone becomes more than a terminal for running commands. It can become a small development environment that you can carry around with you.

#9676. From Front Matter to Index: Pydantic v2, ES/EN Parity and GitHub Actions

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at datalaria.com

In the first article of this series, we exposed the fundamental Achilles' heel of technical content management: the inevitable drift between Git repositories and external databases like Notion or Airtable. We defined the Content Ops as Code philosophy, rooted in treating technical articles and their taxonomy exactly like version-controlled application source code.

However, adopting Git as the Single Source of Truth (SSOT) immediately presents a major software engineering dilemma: Markdown files with YAML front matter lack a type-checking compiler.

A simple typo in a dictionary key (category instead of categories), a publication date stored as free-form unparsed text ("25-11-2026" rather than ISO 2026-11-25), or a tag provided as a raw string instead of a structured list triggers silent rendering failures in modern static site generators such as Hugo, Astro, or Next.js. Worse yet: when managing a bilingual engineering publication across English and Spanish, manually verifying that every translation maintains exact pairing, canonical links, and technical freshness quickly degenerates into an unmanageable bureaucratic maze.

In this article, we break down the internal engineering behind Datalaria Pulse: how we model robust data contracts using Pydantic v2, how we resolve linguistic parity with a deterministic bipartite graph, and how we integrate strict validation into GitHub Actions under an unbreakable rule: if a single metadata field is inconsistent, the pipeline aborts in a closed state (Fail-Closed).

To understand how each piece of the Content Ops as Code architecture fits together, this series consists of 5 structured installments:

The central objective of Datalaria Pulse is to replace manual administrative toil with a deterministic architecture that indexes, validates, and governs technical content assets with zero runtime latency.

Datalaria Pulse applies the same mathematical rigor, interface contracts, and formal governance developed throughout our previous engineering suites and applications:

YAML front matter atop Markdown files (index.md) is convenient for individual writing, but exceptionally fragile as repository scale expands:

When a static generator processes thousands of content lines without schema validation:

To eradicate this risk, we enforce a strict Fail-Closed design: any schema inconsistency immediately aborts local builds and GitHub Actions CI pipelines, preventing malformed assets from ever reaching deployment.

Pydantic v2, rebuilt from the ground up on its compiled Rust core (pydantic-core), delivers the computational performance needed to parse, validate, and compute metrics across hundreds of Markdown assets in fractions of a second.

We define a strict type hierarchy where every editorial entity (whether a Technical Post, an Interactive App, or a Downloadable Kit) is validated against the unified ContentAsset model:

Sustaining bilingual symmetry across dozens of complex engineering posts requires treating content as a bipartite graph where each Spanish node (content/es/posts/) maps directly to its English counterpart (content/en/posts/).

Our ops/pulse/build_index.py engine resolves this pairing through a three-stage matching algorithm:

This classification powers the Bilingual Parity Card in the Datalaria Pulse cockpit (currently standing at 183 / 183 assets, 100% parity), alerting the team if a draft threatens international consistency.

To enforce these invariants without relying on manual diligence, we encapsulate the entire compilation workflow inside a GitHub Actions pipeline triggered on every push to main and on all Pull Requests:

#9674. Razorpay Payment Successful but WooCommerce Order Pending

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at nextgenfusion.in

A customer paid, Razorpay shows the money, and your WooCommerce order still says "Pending payment" or never appeared. The usual cause is not the payment: it is that your store never received, or rejected, Razorpay's server notification (the webhook) that says the payment succeeded. Work through the checks below in order. Most stores find the cause in the first three.

Do not refund automatically and do not ask the customer to pay again until you have checked the payment status in Razorpay.

When a customer pays, two separate messages travel. The first goes through the customer's browser: after payment, the checkout page sends the payment result back to your store. If the customer closes the tab, loses signal or is switched to another app (common with UPI), that message never arrives. The second goes directly from Razorpay's servers to your store: the webhook. Razorpay's documentation describes webhooks as server-to-server notifications sent asynchronously when events occur, such as payment.authorized or order.paid (Razorpay webhooks). It also says that capturing payments for which you did not get a response on the client side is "perhaps the most important use case" for the payment.authorized event. If the browser message fails and the webhook also fails, the order stays pending.

Open the payment in your Razorpay dashboard and note its status.

Open the order and read the notes on the right. Look for lines about the Razorpay payment ID, a signature check or a cancellation. The note "Unpaid order cancelled - time limit reached." means WooCommerce's own unpaid-order timer cancelled the order, which is a different problem: see WooCommerce orders cancelled automatically.

In the Razorpay dashboard, open Webhooks. You need an active webhook that points at your current store address. For the official Razorpay WooCommerce plugin, the webhook address is your site's admin-post.php address with ?action=rzp_wc_webhook added, as set in the plugin's code; the plugin can create the webhook for you when you save its settings. Check that:

If you changed your domain recently, the old webhook may still point to the old one.

Razorpay signs each webhook with your secret, and the signature arrives in the X-Razorpay-Signature header. Razorpay says the signature is calculated with HMAC SHA256, using the webhook secret as the key and the raw request body as the message (validate and test webhooks). If the secret in your Razorpay webhook settings differs from the secret saved in the WooCommerce plugin settings, every webhook fails verification, and the order is never updated. Razorpay also notes that if you change the webhook secret, retries of older events must be validated with the old secret, because the new one causes a mismatch. Re-save the same secret in both places.

Razorpay's request is an HTTP POST from outside your site. These commonly block it:

Check your host's firewall log and your security plugin's blocked-requests log for requests from Razorpay around the payment time.

The plugin's code logs that it handles the payment.authorized event "by cron", and its changelog for version 3.9.4 says "Added delay of 5 minutes to webhook process". So a short delay before the order updates can be normal. If orders stay pending long after that, confirm that WordPress scheduled tasks run. If DISABLE_WP_CRON is set in your configuration, a real server cron job must call wp-cron.php. You can check your plugin version in the plugins list, as behaviour changes between versions.

Razorpay lets you test webhooks in test mode: you can set up a webhook, trigger test events from a test transaction and check whether your endpoint receives them (validate and test webhooks). Run one test payment on your staging copy or in test mode and watch the order notes.

Keep a list so finance can reconcile the orders later.

If the dashboard shows captured payments, the webhook is active, the secrets match, nothing is blocked and orders still do not update, the cause is in code or hosting: a conflicting plugin, a custom checkout, a cache serving old pages to the webhook, or a theme overriding checkout behaviour. A developer can read the plugin's debug log, replay a webhook and trace the request. Our WooCommerce payment integration and checkout troubleshooting covers this, and our guide on WooCommerce orders stuck on pending payment lists causes common to all gateways. See also WooCommerce payment gateways for India.

Not at first. Check the payment status. If it is captured, complete the order. If it is only authorized, capture it or let it be refunded automatically after the window. If it failed, the customer was not charged.

The plugin's changelog mentions a 5-minute delay in webhook processing. Razorpay also polls late authorizations for up to 3 days, so a payment can change status after the customer leaves. If a captured payment still has no matching paid order after 15 to 30 minutes, start the checks above.

UPI payments often involve the customer switching to another app and back. If they do not return to your site, the browser message is lost, and the order relies fully on the webhook.

Yes, after you confirm the payment in the Razorpay dashboard, and add the payment ID as a note. Fix the webhook so you do not have to keep doing it.

The same pattern applies: the browser return can fail, and a verified server notification is the reliable signal. The settings and addresses differ by gateway.

#9673. PageSift 1.7 "Resolve": Stop Trusting Retrieved Text — Verify the Conclusion

PageSift is a Rust web-content engine for LLM pipelines (305 stars, Apache-2.0). Version 1.6 made retrieved text auditable: every passage stored with provenance, version lineage, and an observation timestamp. Version 1.7, released today, adds the layer that was still missing — checking the conclusions you draw from that text.

A retrieval pipeline hands text to a model. The model states conclusions: "the price is $42 a year", "it ships in March", "this tool causes fewer support tickets". Those sentences go into answers, reports, and databases. Nobody checks them.

And they rot. The price changes next month. Two sources disagree and the pipeline keeps whichever it read last. A press release gets copied by five sites and starts to look like five independent confirmations. A study that found a correlation gets quoted as proof of causation. Last year's price gets repeated as today's.

Scraping got the text back. Context (1.6) made the text traceable. The conclusion drawn from it was still taken on faith. Resolve is the layer that checks it.

Say you monitor a product's price. The vendor's page says Widget Pro costs $42 per year. A reseller lists the same product at $45 per year. Your pipeline produces the sentence "Widget Pro costs $42 per year" and you ask Resolve to check it against the stored evidence.

The verdict is conflicted. Resolve tracks support and refutation as separate facts instead of averaging them into a score: one independent source supports the sentence, another independent source refutes it, and the record says exactly that, with citations to both.

Two weeks later the vendor raises the price to $50. The stored conclusion is not left standing. When the underlying evidence changes, Resolve re-checks only the conclusions that depend on the changed passages — and this one flips to refuted, with its full revision history preserved. A conclusion in Resolve is not a one-time judgment. It is a maintained object that stays answerable to its evidence.

1. A conclusion is a stored, versioned record. Each checked answer becomes a ConclusionRecord with one of nine states — supported, supported with qualifiers, refuted, conflicted, insufficient, temporal mismatch, causally unidentifiable, needs human review, observation degraded. Two of those states deserve emphasis: insufficient ("the evidence does not settle this") and causally unidentifiable ("the evidence shows correlation, not causation"). The system is allowed to say it cannot tell, and it does.

2. Checking is deterministic, in seven layers. The checker anchors every claim to its subject, so one product's price can never "confirm" another's. It keeps two time axes apart: when a page was observed versus the period the fact is valid for — a 2024 price cannot confirm a claim about today. It normalizes quantities, currencies, and billing periods, so $42 per month does not confirm $42 per year. It guards negation and dropped qualifiers ("does not include shipping" refutes "includes shipping"; an omitted "unless" downgrades a claim to qualified instead of supported). It refuses causal language on correlational evidence. It collapses copied sources that share one origin, so a syndicated reprint counts once, not five times. And it verifies that every citation actually reaches the passage it claims to support.

3. It argues against itself. After a check, Resolve runs a counter-search: it actively looks for errata, exceptions, and contradicting records that would overturn the conclusion, and attaches an audit of what it searched. The audit states its own limit in plain terms — in an open world, finding no counter-evidence is not proof. Absence of evidence is recorded as absence, never converted into confidence.

4. Conclusions are maintained, not just made. When sources change, an incremental reconciliation finds the affected conclusions and re-verifies only those, cutting off early when a change is a pure relocation or a reconfirmation. In the release evaluation this ran 4.47× faster than full re-verification — which is what makes it practical to re-check every stored conclusion every time its evidence moves, instead of auditing samples once in a while.

The release ships an adversarial evaluation set of 64 cases built to fool a checker: mirror copies, stale prices, billing-period swaps, negation traps, causal overreach. A keyword-overlap baseline — "the words appear in the source, so the claim is supported" — produced a false-support rate of 0.8333. It blessed five out of six wrong answers. Resolve's false-support rate on the same set was 0.0000, with supported precision and recall both at 1.0. In the mirror test, naive source counting gave false support at a rate of 1.0; after origin collapse, 0.

The core check runs at 9,448 checks per second (p50 96µs) on the benchmark machine. That number matters for one reason: verification this cheap does not have to be a nightly audit. It can run on every answer, at the moment the answer is produced.

One honest limitation, from the same evaluation: in deterministic mode, Resolve abstains on heavily metaphorical paraphrases — 3 out of 3 cases came back insufficient, with zero false supports. It would rather say "cannot tell" than guess at what a metaphor means. An optional hybrid mode lets a configured LLM judge those leftovers, but only with verbatim quote grounding, and it can never override a deterministic refutation.

Use Resolve when a conclusion has to stay true: price and spec monitoring, answer auditing for RAG and agent systems, research claims you keep citing, any pipeline where a wrong sentence costs more than the check does.

Do not use it for one-shot scraping. If you fetch a page once and throw the text away, a plain fetch is cheaper and Resolve has nothing to maintain. Its value is entirely in conclusions that live over time and must answer for themselves when the evidence moves.

One implementation, every surface: CLI (pagesift resolve check / reconcile / revalidate / history / graph), HTTP (/v2/resolve*), MCP (pagesift_resolve, 12 tools total), Python and Node SDKs, and a C ABI. Conclusions checked through one surface can be read and maintained through any other.

Where this goes next is a direction, not a promise: from checking conclusions toward computing over evidence. Details when it ships.

#9672. How to Modernize Bank Without Taking Its Payment Systems Offline

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Every bank I have worked with has a system nobody wants to touch.

Sometimes it is a mainframe core banking platform written in COBOL. Sometimes it is a card switch that has been processing ISO 8583 messages reliably for twenty years. Sometimes it is a batch file job that runs at 2 a.m. and that exactly one engineer understands. These systems are old, but they are not broken. They move real money every second.

And yet the business wants mobile apps, open banking APIs, real-time payments and cloud analytics. The question is never "should we modernize?" The question is "how do we modernize without taking the ATM network offline on a Friday payday?"

After roughly sixteen years building ATM, POS and digital banking middleware for banks across the Middle East, Asia and Europe, here is what I have seen actually work.

The tempting plan is to replace the old core in one program. It rarely goes well. Large core replacements have a long public history of delays, outages and customers locked out of their accounts. The reasons repeat:

The alternative is incremental modernization. Less exciting, far more survivable.

Before writing new code, build an inventory of every point where systems talk to each other: protocols (ISO 8583, SWIFT MT/MX, ISO 20022, flat files, SOAP, proprietary TCP), message volumes, peak times, and who owns each interface.

In most banks this map reveals a "spaghetti" of point-to-point links. The ATM switch talks directly to the core. The mobile app calls a SOAP service that calls another SOAP service that writes to a shared database. Every new channel added another direct connection.

You cannot modernize what you have not mapped. You also cannot secure it.

The single most valuable move is introducing a governed integration layer between channels and back-end systems. This can be an API gateway plus a payment middleware or message broker, depending on the flow.

With the layer in place, use the strangler fig pattern: move one business flow at a time from legacy to new, while the rest keeps running untouched.

For each flow, run the new path in shadow mode first: send traffic to both systems, compare results, and only switch over when mismatches are near zero. Keep the routing switch reversible for weeks, not hours.

Integration layers are where security quietly degrades. Patterns I see repeatedly:

This matters well beyond one bank. In the United States, CISA identifies financial services as critical infrastructure, and regulators such as the FFIEC and OCC have repeatedly flagged third-party and legacy integration risk. As U.S. banks connect older cores to real-time rails like the Federal Reserve's FedNow Service and to ISO 20022 messaging, the integration layer becomes the front line of payment security.

During migration, two systems may each believe they own the truth. Automate reconciliation between legacy and new ledgers daily at minimum, and in near real time for payment flows. Every mismatch is either a migration bug or a hidden business rule you did not know about. Both are worth finding before customers do.

Teams celebrate when the new system goes live and forget to decommission the old path. Two systems running forever means double the attack surface and double the cost. For each migrated flow, define:

Legacy banking systems are not the enemy. They are proof that something worked for decades. Modernization succeeds when it respects that, puts a disciplined integration layer between old and new, moves one flow at a time, and treats security and reconciliation as part of the design.

The banks that get this right do not make headlines. Their customers simply never notice the migration happened. That is the goal.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.
