#9581. 8 Trader Joe's Cheeses To Try And 4 To Skip

There's nothing like going to Trader Joe's before hosting a party and stocking up on cool and unusual cheeses. It's the perfect time to try something new or introduce your loved ones to one of your long-standing favorites. Trader Joe's has dozens of cheese at any given time and it can be a little intimidating to narrow down the options. To help out, I sampled some Trader Joe's cheeses to determine which you absolutely need to try, and which you're safe to skip.

None of the cheeses I tried were bad, some just weren't worth it for one reason or another, at a time when we're all watching our budgets extra closely. As touted in Trader Joe's incredibly easy return policy, every single product has been tried (and loved) by a company representative, so the chances of ending up with something that's objectively bad are pretty slim. Still, there were eight truly standout cheeses among my sampling, and four that you can take a pass on. Prices may vary based on your location.

Cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese is not the only fruit studded fresh goat cheese at Trader Joe's, but it was the first one the store introduced, and it persists for good reason! Despite its simple composition (a log of fresh goat cheese rolled in sweetened dried cranberries), it is surprisingly complex. It's creamy, tart, and sweet all at once, and the chewy cranberry pieces keep it texturally interesting. It adds a freshness that can help cut through the other heavy, rich options on your cheeseboard, and it's also super versatile.

If cranberry sauce isn't your preferred vessel for the fruit at the holidays, use this cheese in place of Trader Joe's equally delicious blueberry vanilla goat cheese to make a two-ingredient appetizer with puff pastry sheets. Or, serve the Cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese with dinner and let your guests slather it on their rolls, instead. Perhaps the most inspired option is using the seasonally perfect fresh goat cheese as a spread for your Thanksgiving leftovers sandwich to take it to a whole new level.

Trader Joe's Comté Cheese is the kind of cheese you could expect to find at specialty cheese shop, and probably for a lot more money. That is, in part, because all Comté cheese is subject to Appellation d'Origine Protégée (AOP), which are rules that dictate how and where it is made.

The AOP stamp on Trader Joe's Comté is how you know it's the real deal and follows those same regulations. It's made in just one Alpine region of France (in one of about 134 small villages) using raw milk from one of only two specific breeds of cow, and it is aged for at least four months. The result is a Comté that is firm but creamy, with a somewhat intense smell and a delicately funky flavor. It's definitely one to try, but serve it at room temperature as intended to experience the unique aroma and taste of this strictly-regulated cheese.

Whether or not you have specifically heard of Emmentaler (also called Emmental) cheese, chances are pretty good that you have eaten it. It is the quintessential Swiss cheese that most Americans think of when they hear the term, though there are actually several Swiss cheese varieties.

Trader Joe's Emmentaler has a mild, somewhat sweet and nutty flavor that would be delicious on a ham and Swiss sandwich with Dijon mustard. Emmentaler is even the ultimate fondue cheese. So why is it a skip this time? It does not offer much to set it apart from a Swiss cheese you could buy at any other grocery store. Instead, spend your hard earned money on one of the other kinds of cheese that you can only find exclusively at Trader Joe's. Because, trust us, there are a lot of unique kinds to try at TJ's you can't get anywhere else.

Despite the fact that this Trader Joe's cheese is literally called Unexpected Cheddar Cheese, I'd never tried it, thinking it was just like any other aged cheddar I could buy. I was very wrong (and have since learned my lesson on believing TJ's packaging). There's a reason this cheese came in at No. 2 on our Trader Joe's Product Hall of Fame ranking, and if you've never tried it, now's really the time.

This cheddar has a really nice nuttiness along with its sharp flavor. It is harder and a bit crumblier than many cheddar cheeses, and has those distinctive crunchy crystals typically found more often in varieties like aged Parmigiano-Reggiano. Those crystals are formed during the aging of certain kinds of cheeses, especially in Italy, and are part of what makes Trader Joe's Unexpected Cheddar so delectable. The crumbly texture might not make it the best cheese for slicing up for sandwiches, but you'll enjoy it a hundred different other ways before it even occurs to you to care about that.

Trader Joe's Cheddar Cheese with Caramelized Onions has been my go-to cheese purchase for over a decade, and, all these years later, it still stands up. It has a softer texture than the store's Unexpected Cheddar, so it slices and melts it a bit more easily, but the caramelized onion flavor is where this cheese really shines. There's nothing else like it.

It isn't just onions and cheese, either. The flavor is accomplished by blending a caramelized onion marmalade with an English cheddar cheese. The marmalade has a depth of flavor thanks to cider vinegar, red currant juice, lemon juice, olive oil, clove, cinnamon, and ginger. The warm sweetness of the caramelized onion marmalade is expertly balanced with the salty umami flavor of the cheddar itself, and the little bits of onion throughout make it visually and texturally interesting. This is the ideal cheese to bring to a book club meeting (trust me) and goes well with virtually everything.

The double bottles of bubbly being popped open on the front of this cheese's packaging had me hoping for something celebration worthy, but Trader Joe's English Cheddar Cheese with Champagne just isn't it. It's a perfectly fine cheddar cheese, if a bit on the extra salty side, but I had to really concentrate to pick up on any flavor notes that indicated the presence of Champagne.

According to the ingredients, this cheese includes actual Champagne, as well as Marc de Champagne brandy, which is made by distilling all the parts of the grapes that are leftover after being pressed for Champagne. Still, I had to really search for anything I might call Champagne flavor, which was a letdown. At the end of the day, it just wasn't as delicious as the Unexpected Cheddar or the variety with caramelized onions, despite being the most expensive of the bunch at $12.99 per pound.

I don't think I've ever had a bad Brie, but I can confidently say that I've never had a Brie more delicious than Trader Joe's Triple Cream Brie with Wild Mushrooms. Admittedly, I'm a big fan of mushrooms already, but I'm so used to having Brie with jammy fruits that it never occurred to me that the cheese would really shine when paired with the earthy flavors of wild mushrooms.

Served at room temperature with crackers or crusty bread, it spreads like a dream and needs absolutely nothing to improve it. That said, there's nothing like a baked Brie to make a gathering feel like a party and this wild mushroom variety is no exception. If you're short on time, use your microwave to make a "baked" Brie. You'll still get the delicious, gooey texture everyone loves in baked Brie.

Something I didn't learn until I was in my late 20s is that not everyone eats the rind on Brie, despite the fact that it's completely edible (and delicious). If you're not a fan of the earthy rind, you're probably not going to be a fan of the earthy mushrooms in this cheese, either, but I hope you'll give it a chance.

Trader Joe's Huntsman Cheese looks very different from other options in the cheese case, with its defined white and orange striped layers. Those different stripes are actually two iconic British cheeses: double Gloucester and Blue Stilton.

The two cheeses work together beautifully. The double Gloucester has a smooth flavor with a somewhat firm texture, while the Blue Stilton, which has a Protected Designation of Origin, is sharp and a bit more crumbly (though it's also creamy at room temperature). While the streaks in the Blue Stilton are indeed mold, it's totally scientifically safe to eat the mold in blue cheese.

What I love most about this cheese, other than its very unique appearance that makes it perfect for entertaining, is that its a great introduction to blue cheese for people who are leery of its strong flavor. By pairing the Blue Stilton with the double Gloucester, the flavors are well-balanced while still being complex and delicious. Lure your guests in with the striking appearance and amazing flavor of the Huntsman Cheese, then hit them with the Grand Blue (more on that beauty shortly).

I really wanted to love Trader Joe's Pink Peppercorn Fontina Cheese. It's very eye-catching with its vibrant pink coating and I'd incorrectly assumed that pink peppercorns meant it would be a spicy addition to my cheese selection. Avoid making the same mistake I did and take a minute to learn all about the different kinds of peppercorns, including the fact that pink peppercorns aren't true peppercorns and are more closely related to cashews than black peppercorns.

Still, the company's description of the cheese suggests a level of spice that just wasn't there. Instead, the cheese had an almost sweet vegetal flavor. A closer inspection of the ingredients revealed that the peppercorn seasoning blend also includes freeze dried strawberries, strawberry powder, and dehydrated red bell pepper, which made sense in hindsight. The flavors ended up tasting a bit muddled, though the cheese has some promise if it were paired with the right cracker, fruit, or other accompaniment. While it's certainly pretty, it's not worth the effort to make it truly exceptional.

One of the great things about being someone who is unabashedly a fan of blue cheese is that I never feel bad taking a decent sized serving from a cheese platter at an event. Pair it with a crunchy cracker and some red grapes, and I'm in heaven. But even I didn't know that blue cheese could be as good as Trader Joe's Grand Blue Cheese.

This blue cheese is unbelievably creamy. I would have been hard pressed to crumble it unless it was straight from a very cold refrigerator. At room temperature, it sliced almost like soft butter and spread easily on crackers and bread. This is the blue cheese to serve with a black and blue burger, with the cheese melted on top of the patty, or on a pizza with figs, prosciutto, and a balsamic reduction. It's so creamy that I'd love to try it mixed into mac and cheese, if I can manage to make it last long enough next time I buy it (but the need to eat it straight-up might win out).

Havarti is a creamy Danish cheese that holds up super well to both slicing and melting, which makes it a great addition to recipes and on your cheese board. It has a relatively mild, somewhat sweet flavor that lends well to the addition of herbs, peppers, and spices. Perhaps the most iconic variety is Havarti with dill, and Trader Joe's version is worth adding to your shopping list.

Fresh dill is used in a lot of Nordic and Scandinavian cooking, so it makes sense that it's a perfect companion to a Danish cheese like Havarti. Trader Joe's Havarti with dill is absolutely packed with the bright herb. If you're the type of person who loves anything dill pickle flavored, you're going to love this cheese. Add it to anything that could use an herbaceous boost, but I highly recommend pairing it with Trader Joe's Unexpected Cheddar for a grilled cheese sandwich that's out of this world. For a bright crunch that brings out the cheese's sweetness, add some crisp apple slices, too. Thank me later.

Prior to trying Trader Joe's Toscano Cheese Dusted With Cinnamon, I'd never actually heard of Toscano cheese. It turns out that that's because it's based on another cheese entirely, with a few important differences. Interestingly enough, while the retailer carries other cheeses with protected status, its Toscano is an interpretation rather than a faithful rendering of Italian Pecorino Toscano, which has a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO).

Italian Pecorino Toscano is a sheep's milk cheese made primarily in Tuscany, while Trader Joe's Toscano (both this cinnamon dusted version and other varieties it offers) are made from cow's milk in Wisconsin. There's nothing inherently wrong with either of those characteristics, and the cinnamon dusting on the cheese gives it a pleasantly warm sweetness, but it feels a bit like a bait and switch. The retailer describes the cheese as being like cheddar in texture and Parmesan in flavor, but I found that it was kind of bland compared to other options, and not even the dusting of cinnamon made it worth the buy.

To ensure a wide range of Trader Joe's cheese, I gathered varieties from all around the world and across many cheese-making styles. While I would happily sample every variety Trader Joe's has to offer, I stuck to a budget of $75, which still allowed me to splurge on a few options and sample a total of 12 cheeses.

Each cheese was tried  first on its own to allow its natural flavor profile a chance to shine. Initial impressions were gathered based on how much I enjoyed the cheese, how much of it I wanted to keep eating, and whether it felt worth it for the cost. That last criterion included considerations like whether the cheese was memorable and how excited I would be to introduce it to a friend. The following day, I prepared a cheese board with all of the cheese samples, two types of crackers, and warm toasted baguette, which I enjoyed with my husband while watching television to solidify my recommendations.

#9578. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9577. Scrambled Eggs Are 10x Tastier When You Add One Store-Bought Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When you're a fan of eggs, they can be pretty delicious however it is that they come off the stove or out of the oven. Even so, sometimes you're in the mood for something that doesn't require a lot of preparation yet is adaptable and tastes delicious. That's where scrambled eggs come in. They have a beautiful texture — whether you like them super soft and slightly gooey or a bit on the crispy side. There are a lot of different techniques, and some ways to cook them are better than others – like cooking them in water is probably a bad idea. Following some expert tips for scrambled eggs can get you to full-on restaurant quality; for example, fresh eggs at room temperature will give you great-tasting results that cook evenly. But when you want to keep it super simple at home, you can improve your everyday scrambled eggs by adding in a little bouillon.

Either beef or chicken bouillon will work. Beef bouillon will give your eggs a deep, unctuous taste that can be delicious, but may be a bit heavy if you're not looking for something super bold. Using a little chicken bouillon, on the other hand, will add some bright, salty notes that still have plenty of extra umami. Chicken bouillon will bring out the natural savory, even slightly sweet flavor of the eggs without overpowering them — which makes sense because they're both, well, chicken. Whichever you choose to use, bouillon makes a super easy addition to your scrambled eggs that really only takes a few extra seconds of work.

As far as the bouillon goes, really anything will work — although it is often easier to get exact smaller measurements with powdered jars or pastes, like Better Than Bouillon Premium Roasted Chicken Base. Most standard bouillon cubes are equal to 1 teaspoon of bouillon powder or paste, but it can differ between brands, so take a look at the label. You'll want about a quarter teaspoon per three eggs. You can simply whisk the bouillon into the raw eggs with whatever seasonings and dairy you'd normally use (although you may want to lay off extra sodium because it's already quite salty), then scramble them to your preference. You can even wait to add the bouillon until the eggs have begun to set, then remove them from the heat and fold in the bouillon, so it just sort of melts in.

If you want to go beyond milk or cream, you can try it with a little crème fraîche, sour cream, or cream cheese, or even a Gruyère or sharp cheddar. Pepper is a must to bring out your egg's full potential, and you might want to even try a pinch of sugar for a hit of sweetness that blends in nicely — especially with chicken bouillon. As for the veggies and herbs, this trick will go great with pretty much everything you usually like to see in your eggs; just consider the flavor profile if you're using beef versus chicken. You can even use canned veggies in your scramble; for example, canned tomatoes are subtly sweet and tangy, pairing excellently with chicken bouillon while canned mushrooms add umami and even more depth to beef.

#9575. The Best American Burger Chain Isn't Shake Shack Or Five Guys

As one of America's favorite fast food items, burgers are something you've almost certainly ordered from a chain at least once in your life — but not all chains are created equal. Everyone has a favorite, so the question of which is best is bound to stir up some fiery debate. Even so, we didn't let that stop us from ranking nine of America's favorite burger chains, and coming out on top of our list was Culver's.

Founded in Sauk City, Wisconsin, Culver's now has more than 1,000 locations across more than two dozen U.S. states. Its flagship item, the ButterBurger, is served on a fluffy Kaiser bun, and customers have the option to customize it with a long list of toppings, including some world-class Wisconsin cheese slices. Living up to its founding state's nickname as America's Dairyland, Culver's treats dairy as a core part of the menu. Its famous Wisconsin Cheese Curds arrive breaded and gooey, while its fresh frozen custard is the perfect way to round off a meal.

Culver's uses fresh, never-frozen beef, with its cooked-to-order patties made from a flavorful blend of sirloin, chuck, and plate. But what really sets it apart from chains like Shake Shack and Five Guys is the seasoning. Culver's uses salt and pepper, while Five Guys forgoes seasoning altogether. The chain argues its beef is so good that seasoning is unnecessary, but not all customers buy that reasoning.

Meanwhile, Shake Shack does season its patties, but Culver's has one not-so-secret ingredient that tips the scales in its favor: butter. It's spread on the crown of the bun, which is then toasted until golden, adding a rich flavor that makes the bun just as tasty as the patty.

While the taste and quality of food certainly play a major role in where we rank a chain, they aren't the only factors to consider. On Reddit, one customer shared why they love Culver's: "[It's] probably the best [all-around] fast food there is," they claimed. "[High-quality] ingredients, consistent, always hot[,] and the restaurants are always clean." Which brings us to one seriously underappreciated category: cleanliness.

Just think about it: A good meal can quickly be soured by a grimy dining area. Fast food often gets a bad rap for the quality of its food, but when it comes to hygiene, the best chains can easily hold their own against high-end sit-down restaurants. Culver's is no exception, and customers and media outlets have even credited it with having some of the cleanest bathrooms in the fast food game, which can only be a good thing.

Beyond cleanliness, Culver's is also one of the few major fast food chains left that's still family-owned. Rather than answering to shareholders, the company still has co-founder Craig Culver as its chairman. This has seen Culver's put plenty back into its community, most notably through its Thank You Farmers Project; the chain's website states that it has helped raise more than $8 million for agricultural education since 2013. Much of that comes from Scoops of Thanks Day, when customers get a scoop of custard in exchange for a $1 donation to their local Future Farmers of America chapter.

#9573. 8 Fish With More Protein Than Salmon

Unless you've been living under a rock, you'll know that protein-maxxing is all the rage right now. The conversation largely revolves around go-to options like chicken breast, but we'll let you in on a little-known secret: Several meats out there actually outrank poultry when it comes to the macronutrient. Among them are certain types of fish, a protein source that often gets sidelined in the conversation, but leaving it out would be a serious mistake. Aside from being delicious, versatile, and (much of the time) budget-friendly, fish is also seriously easy to cook.

Salmon may be the most popular high-protein fish, and 100 grams of the farmed Atlantic variety contains around 20.3 grams of protein. That's already impressive, since it beats the 18.2 grams found in the same amount of 90% lean ground beef and comes up just under 2 grams shy of chicken breast. Compared to other fish, however, salmon actually gets outdone.

Tuna sits at or near the very top of the seafood protein hierarchy thanks to its lean, muscular build, but beyond whole fish, another serious source of protein is the canned variety. At face value, a tiny, oily anchovy isn't much to look at. But once these fish are packed tightly into cans, you're left with a surprisingly concentrated source of protein, along with a healthy dose of other beneficial nutrients. If anchovies pack too much of a punch for your taste, canned sardines also make for an excellent high-protein swap — and that's only the beginning.

Salty, briny, and often budget-friendly, canned anchovies contain a whopping 25.4 grams per 100-gram serving. You can enjoy them straight from the can since they're already cured, or if you want to take a more elevated approach, take a cue from the Portuguese and use them as an elegant garnish on toast alongside capers, good-quality olive oil, pickled red onions, and a sprinkling of parsley for good measure.

Sardines might be tiny, but they're loaded with protein (around 24 grams per 100 grams, to be precise). Like anchovies, they're an oily, nutrient-rich fish, but they set themselves apart with a milder, less salty flavor. Often sold whole, they make for a visually appealing garnish if you're looking to add a little drama to your dishes, and since canned sardines have already been cooked, they're good to eat straight out of the tin.

Yellowfin tuna, also known as ahi, is one of the more premium tuna species out there. Alongside its firm, beef-like texture and clean flavor, it's loaded with protein, with a 100-gram serving containing around 24.7 grams. It's also exceptionally versatile, since suppliers cut it into loins, saku blocks, and steaks for a hearty meal, while thinly sliced or cubed pieces work wonders in a tropical poke bowl or as delicious nigiri if you're craving something lighter.

Bluefin is the undisputed king of tuna; it's prized for sushi and sashimi, and its price can reach heights that can only be described as absurd — a 612-pound bluefin once sold for $3 million at a 2019 Tokyo auction. Like its price, its protein content sits on the higher end of the spectrum, too, reaching roughly 23 grams per 100-gram serving. But bluefin is better known for its impressive fat content, with the fatty otoro belly especially prized for its smooth, buttery texture.

Tilapia is one of the most popular fish in America, and despite its bargain price tag, it delivers a serious amount of protein, with a 100-gram serving containing 26.2 grams. It's also a solid pick if you've got sustainability in mind, since responsibly farmed tilapia can be relatively easy on the environment. This lean whitefish has a firm, flaky texture and mild flavor that stands up beautifully to grilling or pan-searing, making for a quick and satisfying weeknight dinner.

Halibut is a fan favorite that just edges out salmon's protein content, with approximately 20.8 grams per 100 grams. Despite those similar protein profiles, halibut is a lower-fat alternative with a considerably less fishy taste, making it a popular pick for those who have yet to come around on salmon. There are plenty of ways to prepare it, and grilling, pan-frying, or baking will all make for a delicious meal.

Notable for its vibrant red skin, firm white flesh, and uniquely sweet, nutty flavor, red snapper is a hugely popular seafood choice that packs 20.51 grams of protein per 100-gram serving. Compared to your everyday whitefish, its price tag ranges from moderate to expensive, but it more than makes up for it with a wonderfully tender texture. To make use of its dramatic red hue, pair your snapper with seasonings and aromatics and bake it whole.

If you've grown tired of salmon's ever-rising price tag, look no further than rainbow trout. Also available as steelhead trout, this seriously underrated fish has a milder, more delicate flavor than salmon and leaner, finer-flaked flesh. Rainbow trout contains 20.5 grams of protein per 100-gram serving, though its leaner profile makes it less forgiving than salmon at very high heat, so it's best suited to gentler methods like pan-frying or whole roasting.

#9569. Forget Plain Bacon: Add This Crispy Ingredient To Grilled Cheese For Sweet & Smoky Flavor

Plain old bacon can elevate even the plainest grilled cheese, but it tends to be a bit one-note, contributing mainly salty, crispy protein. However, if you add candied bacon instead, that extra sweetness can transform a wide variety of cheeses and breads, especially if you take the time to prepare it with extra seasonings.

Candied bacon is a delicate recipe, but if you manage to make it without burning the sugars, you get an incomparably delicious ingredient for grilled cheese. The syrupy sweetness helps cut through the sodium, whether from aged parmesan or bread crusted with garlic salt, and the texture provides a nice contrast to gooey cheese. The smokiness, in particular, is a great flavoring agent that you can easily control by increasing or reducing the amount of bacon you layer on. The end result is a nice middle ground between turning grilled cheese into a dessert and keeping it exclusively savory.

Candied bacon can take a hot minute to prepare and cook, and while it only lasts about a week in the fridge, it stays good in the freezer for up to six months. Since all you have to do is let it thaw, then zap it in the air fryer for a few minutes at 380 degrees Fahrenheit, it's a superbly easy accoutrement to keep on hand for when you want something a little special.

The best part of using candied bacon is that while it may close a few flavor doors, it opens up so many more. You may not want to pair it with an herbed goat cheese or wine-veined cheddar, but it can substantially upgrade many of the tastiest underrated cheeses into something spectacular.

When considering what to add to your new sandwich, try to think about the types of cheeses you'd find in desserts. Something creamy and high in fat provides fantastic texture and an aromatic backdrop of flavor but still lets the candied bacon take center stage. Brie, Camembert, and mascarpone are all sublime with a bit of sugar, but when balanced with the savoriness of cured bacon, they become even better. Any pale, rich variety should do the job well.

You should always use a variety of cheeses in your grilled cheese, and a dash of something sharp and aged can balance out the powerful flavors of candied bacon. Microplaning some aged Manchego or provolone on top diversifies the flavors without overpowering them, and the extra-fine texture helps even harder cheeses melt more evenly. While you don't want these to be the main characters of your recipe, a bit of added nuttiness and earthiness can bring out the best in your bacon, even if you only add a tablespoon or two.

#9568. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

#9567. 5 Types Of Brain-Affecting Drugs Still Prescribed Despite Safety Warnings

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.

These drugs can increase the risk of confusion, falls and hospitalisation, particularly in people whose thinking and memory are already impaired.

Despite decades of warnings, people with cognitive impairment were more likely to receive these prescriptions than those with normal cognition.

The research examined five categories of medication flagged by prescribing guidelines for older adults:

Only antidepressants with strong anticholinergic properties were included in this category.

Anticholinergic medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, learning and concentration.

Blocking its action can cause confusion and other unwanted effects, especially in older adults.

Benzodiazepines, which may be prescribed for anxiety or sleep problems, can cause excessive drowsiness and increase the risk of falls.

Some medicines also take longer to leave the body as people age, allowing their effects to persist or accumulate.

The researchers analysed survey information linked to medical insurance records from almost 4,900 Americans aged 65 and over.

They examined prescribing over nine years, counting prescriptions for at least four weeks’ supply.

Around 17 percent of people with normal cognition received at least one potentially inappropriate prescription, compared with almost 22 percent of those with cognitive impairment without dementia.

Among people with dementia, the proportion reached 25 percent.

Across the older adults studied, prescribing fell from around 20 percent at the beginning of the study period to 16 percent at the end.

Much of the decline reflected fewer prescriptions for benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping medicines.

However, prescribing rates for the other three drug groups did not change significantly.

By the final year, more than two-thirds of people receiving these potentially inappropriate prescriptions lacked a documented clinical reason for at least one of them.

A potentially inappropriate medicine can still be justified when its expected benefits outweigh its risks.

The practical question is whether each prescription remains suitable for the person taking it.

Dr Annie Yang, the study’s first author, emphasised the importance of patients and carers reviewing these medicines with their physicians:

“While CNS-active prescriptions may be appropriate in some cases, it is important for older patients or their caregivers to work closely with their physicians to ensure that these medications are appropriate to their cases.

When inappropriate, patients and their care teams should consider alternative treatments and consider whether it might be safe to taper or stop the medication.”

The study was published in JAMA (Yang et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the United States. That is about 17% of all US households — roughly 1 in 6. And the number is growing: the US added over 2 million new millionaire households between 2019 and 2022 alone, even through a global pandemic.

But here is what might surprise you: most millionaires do not look like what you expect. They are not driving Ferraris or living in mansions. The research — most notably from Thomas Stanley and William Danko's landmark study "The Millionaire Next Door" and Chris Hogan's follow-up study of over 10,000 millionaires — consistently shows that the typical American millionaire is a middle-aged person with a modest lifestyle who has been saving and investing for 25-30 years.

This matters for the FI community because it proves that building a million-dollar net worth is not about luck, inheritance, or extraordinary income. It is about consistent behavior applied over time. And if you are on the FI path, you are following the exact same playbook that created 22 million millionaires.

The exact number depends on how you measure it and which data source you use:

The discrepancy between 22 million and 14-15 million comes down to whether you include home equity. If you count total net worth (including home equity), approximately 22 million households qualify. If you count only investable assets (excluding the primary residence), the number drops to about 14-15 million.

For FI purposes, investable assets are the more meaningful measure — your home equity does not fund your retirement spending unless you sell or downsize. But by either measure, the US has more millionaires than any other country in the world.

Note: Growth includes both new wealth creation and inflation. A million dollars in 2000 had the purchasing power of approximately $1.8 million in 2024 dollars.

Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (the largest ever conducted) surveyed over 10,000 millionaires and found: 79% received zero inheritance. The top occupations were engineer, accountant, teacher, management, and attorney — not entrepreneurs or celebrities. 96% said anyone can become a millionaire with discipline and consistent investing. The average millionaire started investing at age 29 and became a millionaire at 49. They are your neighbors, not the people on magazine covers.

The research paints a consistent picture of the typical American millionaire — and it looks very different from what pop culture suggests.

Sources: Chris Hogan National Study of Millionaires, Thomas Stanley "The Millionaire Next Door", Federal Reserve SCF

The path to millionaire status in America overwhelmingly follows a formula, not a lottery ticket:

Millionaires are not "the 1%" — they are the top 10-15%. Here is how wealth is distributed across US households:

Source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, 2022

This means approximately 16% of American households have a net worth of $1 million or more. And the pathway from $500K-$1M (where 11% of households sit) to the millionaire club is often just a matter of continuing to do what they are already doing for another 5-10 years.

The answer depends entirely on two variables: how much you invest each month and what rate of return you earn. Using a conservative 7% average annual real return (the stock market's historical average adjusted for inflation):

Assumes 7% average annual real return with monthly compounding. Results are in today's dollars.

The most striking column is "Growth" — at every savings level, compound growth does a significant portion of the work. An investor saving $1,000/month reaches $1 million in 26 years, but $688,000 of that is investment growth, not contributions. That is the power of compound interest working over decades in low-cost index funds.

FI community members reach millionaire status faster than the average American millionaire (age 49) for three reasons:

A household earning $100,000 with a 50% savings rate ($50,000/year invested) will reach $1 million in approximately 13-14 years at 7% real returns. That is financial independence by age 40-45 if they start at 28-30. This is not theoretical — thousands of FI community members have documented this exact trajectory.

If you are pursuing financial independence, you are on the millionaire path by design. Here is why:

The standard FI formula is 25x your annual spending. If your household spends $40,000 per year, your FI number is $1,000,000 — you are literally targeting millionaire status. If you spend $60,000, your number is $1.5 million. If you spend $80,000, it is $2 million.

Every FI practitioner is building toward a net worth that exceeds $1 million. The difference between the FI community and the general millionaire population is intentionality: FI community members know their number, track their progress monthly, and optimize their savings rate to get there as quickly as possible.

The data from "The Millionaire Next Door" and subsequent research validates the FI approach completely: live below your means, invest the difference in diversified low-cost funds, avoid debt, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting over 15-25 years. That is the millionaire formula. It is also the FI formula. They are the same thing.

The data says this works. 22 million households have already proven it.

Multiply your annual spending by 25. That is your target net worth. For most FI-minded households, this will be $1-2.5 million — squarely in millionaire territory.

Pro tip: Use your ACTUAL spending, not your income. Spending $50,000/year means you need $1.25 million, regardless of whether you earn $60K or $200K.

The average millionaire lived on 75% of their income during accumulation years. FI community members target 30-60%. Every percentage point increase in savings rate accelerates your timeline.

Set up automatic monthly investments into a total stock market index fund. Max out your 401(k) match first, then Roth IRA, then taxable brokerage. Do not try to pick stocks — even professional fund managers fail at this 90% of the time.

73% of millionaires have never carried a credit card balance. Pay off any existing high-interest debt aggressively, then commit to paying your credit card in full every month. Consumer debt is the single biggest destroyer of wealth-building momentum.

Every millionaire tracked their progress. Calculate your net worth on the first of each month and chart the trend. The visual feedback loop of watching your number grow is the most powerful motivator on the path to seven figures.

If you are saving 20% or more of your income and investing it in index funds, you are following the exact playbook that created 22 million millionaire households. The only question is timing. At a 30% savings rate, you will get there in approximately 22 years. At 50%, approximately 17 years. The formula is proven, the math is clear, and thousands of FI community members have walked this path before you.

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the US based on total net worth (assets minus liabilities, including home equity), according to the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances. If you exclude primary residence equity and count only investable assets, the number is approximately 14-15 million households. Either way, the US has more millionaires than any other country.

Approximately 17% of US households have a net worth of $1 million or more. That is roughly 1 in 6 households. If measuring only investable assets (excluding home equity), approximately 11-12% of households qualify. The percentage has been growing steadily — it was about 7% in 2000.

Overwhelmingly self-made. Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (10,000+ surveyed) found that 79% received zero inheritance. Only 3% received an inheritance over $1 million. The primary wealth-building mechanism was consistent investing in employer-sponsored retirement plans (401(k)s and IRAs) over 25-30 years. The myth that most wealthy people inherited their money is not supported by the data.

The average American millionaire reaches $1 million in net worth at age 49, according to multiple studies. However, this average includes people who started investing late. FI community members who begin saving 30-50% of their income in their 20s frequently reach millionaire status by their late 30s or early 40s — a decade ahead of the average.

Yes, but it requires discipline and time. Saving 20% of a $50,000 salary ($10,000/year or $833/month) invested at 7% real returns would reach $1 million in approximately 30 years. Increasing savings to 30% ($15,000/year) compresses the timeline to approximately 25 years. It is slower than higher earners, but it is mathematically achievable — and many millionaires built their wealth on middle-class incomes.

$1 million supports $40,000/year in spending at a 4% safe withdrawal rate. Add average Social Security benefits ($22,884/year for a retired worker in 2024), and that is about $62,884/year. Whether this is "enough" depends on your location and lifestyle. In a moderate cost-of-living area, it is comfortable. In San Francisco or New York City, it is tight. The FI community recommends calculating YOUR specific number based on YOUR spending — $1 million is a milestone, not necessarily a finish line.

There are 22 million millionaire households in the US — and the data consistently shows they got there through consistent saving and investing, not inheritance, luck, or extraordinary income. The average millionaire earned a solid but not exceptional income, lived below their means, invested in diversified funds for 25-30 years, and avoided consumer debt. If that description sounds familiar, it should — it is the exact blueprint the FI community follows. You do not need to be born wealthy or earn a six-figure salary to join the millionaire club. You need a savings rate above 20%, a low-cost index fund, and enough time for compound growth to do its work. The 22 million millionaires before you have proven it works.

#9565. Skip Soy Sauce: Marinate Steak In This Umami Ingredient For A Delicious Flavor Boost

People love soy sauce for a next-level steak marinade not just because of its salt, but also its complexity. If, however, you want to eschew the sodium and bump up that deliciously fermented flavor, you need koji, a type of rice critical to Japanese sake production.

When you inoculate short-grain rice with Aspergillus oryzae mold, it slowly breaks down proteins and carbohydrates into an ingredient you can then ferment for sake or dry for use as a savory, shelf-stable ingredient. This is koji, a lesser-known source of umami that is nonetheless a potent marinade ingredient. While the differences are more subtle than with soy sauce, it gives you great control over your meat's final flavor profile and leaves you room to add other seasonings, like the best salts for seasoning steak, herbs, and spices.

If you use shio koji, a type of marinade made by combining koji rice with salt and water, you can even tenderize your meat. The sodium helps the beef retain moisture, while the enzymes break down proteins, leaving your steak tender and flavorful no matter how you prepare it. Just be careful, as some varieties have added sugars that can unexpectedly sweeten your meat too much. While they won't exactly candy your steak, they might overhaul your food's taste.

Whether you use wet shio koji or dry, shelf-stable koji, this ingredient is extremely useful and easy to add to marinades. Just keep in mind that its enzymes remain active when wet, so you'll want to be careful about how long you let your steak sit before cooking.

Dry, shelf-stable koji is quite versatile but may require extra steps. Grinding it into a powder and adding a few tablespoons to your marinade is a great way to boost umami. However, you can also create a dry crust on your steak and let it sit in your fridge for a couple of days. This can mimic some of the effects of long dry-aging, helping your beef develop an impressive level of complexity in only 48 hours. However, you'll want to rinse the rice off your meat and pat it dry before cooking, as its starches and natural sugars burn quite easily.

Shio koji is a bit easier to use and so delicious that you don't even need other marinade ingredients. Since it's able to thoroughly coat the meat, this is a great choice if you're working with tough cuts, like flank steak, that need some extra tenderizing. Two tablespoons per pound of protein should be plenty to get tender meat. To get a good crust, you'll still want to wipe off the excess rice and moisture and watch your heat, but it's an otherwise hands-off recipe that can taste like you spent hours fretting over the perfect marinade.

#9562. Not Cocoa Powder Or Coffee: Add This Pantry Staple To Canned Chili For A Major Flavor Boost

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A good chili is a solid meal in a bowl that can be made easily at home in the slow cooker. It takes a lot of time, but it can create meals for days. There are plenty of different types of chili to enjoy if you want to try something new. But when you don't want to spend the time in the kitchen with all the beef browning and veggie prep, you can grab a pre-made chili right off the grocery store shelf. Some swear by coffee or cocoa powder to upgrade your chili, but there's one ingredient you likely have in the pantry or fridge that you probably have never considered. To improve the flavor of your canned chili, you should add a touch of jam or jelly as you heat it up.

Adding a fruit jelly or jam to your canned chili will help build complexity and draw out the flavor of common seasonings found in the dish — like cumin, paprika, cayenne, chili, and garlic and onion powders — while also offering a bit of contrast. It's like adding a pinch of brown sugar, with just a skosh of bright, fruit-forward undertones that can make it taste more like it's fresh, homemade, with subtle nuance usually lost in canned goods. It also helps cut the acidity of the tomato sauce that may sometimes be overpowering, especially in canned chili. Using a bit of the jarred stuff will even improve the look of your meal, adding a nice gloss or top sheen to give you an end result that looks like something right out of the page of a cookbook.

If you want to go with something gourmet that's relatively easy to find, a jar of Bonne Maman Strawberry Preserves, available online and at retailers like Walmart, will work nicely, but you can use homemade preserves or pretty much any store-bought jam or jelly, like Smucker's Concord Grape Jelly, also available online and in stores. In fact, jellies are often preferred because they blend in seamlessly, and you won't end up with over-sweet chunks of fruit in your chili. If you plan to use something with whole fruit, you may want to simmer it for longer on the stove, so the chili flavor will fully infuse with it. Grape is a pretty solid choice because it will beautifully complement the deep umami flavor of the beef without overpowering it. Fig and apricot jams also work great for some added depth and earthiness.

When it comes to your base, not all canned chilis are created equal, but this trick will definitely add flavor to whatever you choose to use. You'll want to start with about a half teaspoon of jam or jelly per can as you heat up the chili, then give it a taste once it's simmering. If it's not quite there, you can always add more, but hold back from going too hard right out of the gate.

Because of the extra sweetness, you may need an extra pinch of salt — although most canned chilis are already pretty sodium-rich. And some spicy additions, like fresh or canned jalapeños, red pepper flakes, or a dash of hot sauce, will balance things out nicely.

#9561. The best Thanksgiving baking tips from Ina Garten, Erin McDowell, and more pro bakers: Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.

It’s the most wonderful baking season of the year, and to help you bake your best, we have top tips from some of the country’s best bakers, pulled from conversations on the Things Bakers Know podcast. Below, you’ll find Thanksgiving strategies from upcoming podcast guests Ina Garten (episode dropping November 23!) and King Arthur’s Martin Philip (find his episode November 16), as well as guests from previously aired episodes, including Erin McDowell, Helen Goh, and many more of our baking friends.

“The one thing I think people think they can do is multiply a recipe times four and think it’s going to come out fine, which it won’t,” Ina shared on her forthcoming podcast episode. Instead of taking one recipe and just multiplying by three or four, she suggests either baking the original recipe multiple times, or doubling it and baking two or three times, depending on how many people you’re feeding. Just don’t multiply more than once! If you do, the leavening and flavoring starts to get thrown off.

If you’re baking for a lot of people, Ina also suggests making recipes scaled for a baking sheet. As she explains, “It’s easier to bake, and it’s easier to cut.” We’d recommend Slab Chocolate Pecan Pie, Pumpkin Cake Bars with Cream Cheese Frosting, or Walnut and Oat Slab Pie.

While you may be excited to try out a show-stopping recipe from a brand-new cookbook, Ina recommends resisting temptation. “You don’t want to test something you haven’t made a million times,” she cautions. “Even for me, it adds enormous stress.” Instead of turning to a first-time recipe, Ina highly recommends that you “do the things you know will come out perfectly every time.” And if you do want to make a new-to-you recipe this Thanksgiving, consider baking it once or twice in the weeks leading up to the holiday, so you have the chance to practice and work out any kinks (like figuring out make-ahead components or fridge storage) before hosting on the big day.

No one wants a soggy bottom on their pie, especially a super-juicy one like apple pie. Erin McDowell has lots of tips to avoid a soggy bottom, but her biggest one is to precook your apple filling before assembling your pie. “We can't necessarily predict how juicy any given fruit is, so even if you're using the same apple … each time, they are going to be a little bit different,” she explained on our podcast episode all about apples. Precooking the filling allows you to adjust based on the juiciness of the fruit you’re using that day. “If you're dealing with not-very-juicy apples, you may not have to cook it as long. If they're really juicy, you may have to cook it longer, but the process is the same.”

Pie crust can be incredibly intimidating for some bakers. But pie queen Stacey Mei Yan Fong says the key to success is sometimes to chill out, figuratively and literally. “The best thing you can do is just chill, as in calm down. You're not doing brain surgery,” she reminded Jessica in our Thanksgiving pie episode. “And also use your fridge!” As she points out, “the minute things start getting too wet or things start getting too warm, that's when people panic.” So take a moment to chill the dough and make it easier to work with. If the butter's getting soft or your pie dough is getting difficult to work with, just put it in the fridge to cool down for 10 to 15 minutes.

It’s not just the fridge, either — your freezer can also be incredibly helpful. Stacey likes to freeze her pies before baking, which she says helps the crimping hold its shape as it bakes. And remember that, as Stacey points out, “Pie is kind of a lesson in patience.”

On our special Holiday Q+A Extravaganza dropping November 23, King Arthur’s Director of Baking Education Amber Eisler has a crucial tip for avoiding runny apple pies — make sure you see your pie filling actively bubbling through the vents in your pie crust. As she explains, “It means the filling has boiled and bubbled, so the starches in the filling are actually thickening, which is a super important part of [avoiding a soupy pie].”

There’s a lot of cooking and baking happening around Thanksgiving, which means your oven can get pretty crowded, pretty quickly. But be wary of overfilling it. Even though your oven may have up to three racks inside, Martin Philips cautions against using them all at the same time. “Don’t make the mistake of crowding the oven when it comes to rolls. Let bread have its moment,” he says. Bake your pies the day before to save oven space; a turkey, too will stay hot out of the oven for hours. When baking rolls, you want “top and bottom heat, use your convection setting, make sure that air is moving,” says Martin. “Guard the rolls, y’all!”

Cookbook author and professional psychologist Helen Goh believes in the power of baking to bring meaning and fulfillment to our lives. During this busy holiday season, full of messy kitchens, family squabbles, lengthy to-do lists, and lots of hosting, it can be easy to get overwhelmed. But baking can actually be a calming, comforting activity right now. “Some people say baking makes them nervous because you have to focus,” says Helen. But part of the therapeutic effect of baking comes from forcing us to focus on a single task at hand. As she points out, “that takes you away from all that white noise about what you did yesterday or what's going to happen tomorrow,” and instead allows you to live mindfully in the moment.

Happy Thanksgiving from all of us here at King Arthur. If you run into baking troubles or just need a little support in the kitchen, our Baker’s Hotline is here to help.

#9560. Add This Packet Of Seasoning To Pot Roast For A Delicious Southern-Style Sandwich

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Pot roast is one of those simple homemade meals that may take a long time to cook but is pretty hands-off in the Crock Pot. Just brown the meat, add your ingredients, and let the cooker do its job. There are plenty of ways to upgrade a basic pot roast and some interesting regional pot roast dishes, and this simple trick is a bit of both. To give your pot roast a hint of Southern twang, add a packet of dry ranch seasoning. Similar to a set-it-and-forget-it easy French dip sandwich but Southern, a bit of ranch in your pot roast will give you some delightfully intense flavor and get you darn near a classic Mississippi pot roast.

Ranch seasoning is basically an off-the-shelf, ready-to-go spice packet containing multiple seasonings — usually salt, onion powder, garlic powder, and other dried herbs and spices, like parsley and black pepper. Most brands also contain buttermilk and whey, which will add a bit of a creaminess factor, but you don't have to worry about the roast tasting like a bottle of ranch dressing because the mix will cook down with added beef stock and natural juices to form a nice, thick gravy. It will come out rich, bold, and savory with just a hint of tanginess from the buttermilk. Once your roast is nice and tender, you can simply slice it (or shred it) up and serve it Italian-beef or French-dip style, preferably with some melted cheese on top. The first bite through the bread into the perfectly tender and umami-rich, seasoned beef will make you a believer.

If you want to go for a more or less standard pot roast route, you can simply rub your roast with a packet of Hidden Valley Ranch Seasoning, available online and in stores, or something similar, and cook it how you normally would with beef stock, potatoes, onions, carrots, and whatever other veg you like to use. To go full-on Mississippi roast, you can forgo the veggies and slow cook it with the ranch coating, beef stock or au jus gravy mix, and a half dozen or more whole pepperoncini. Up the spice level with extra hot peppers or use the whole jar. You can even add a bit of the brine for some supplementary heat, plus a zingy kick of vinegar. This will get you closer to an actual Mississippi pot roast, which typically features said peppers.

For the bread, something that will hold up to the moisture of the roast is ideal. Toasted French bread adds a crunchy texture, but a toasted hoagie roll works great, and a thick sourdough will add a little extra tang. You'll want a cheese that melts easily, so you can quickly broil it without overcooking the bread. A simple mozzarella is an easy, mild choice, but a nice Gruyère will bring a richer and nuttier flavor with some subtle sweetness.

Ranch-seasoned pot roast or the full Mississippi mix is also great on egg noodles, mashed potatoes, or rice, or you can make a simple open-faced sando with a thick Texas toast. For an even saltier, more savory roast, you can try a three-packet blend with ranch, brown gravy, and Italian-style salad dressing mixes. However, to get that good Southern flavor, don't veer too far off the ranch.

#9559. How to turn any bread dough into rolls: Transform your favorite bread loaf into shareable rolls.

So you have a beloved bread recipe that you'd like to turn into fluffy, single-serving rolls, but you don’t know where to start. We’re here to help — let’s get rolling!

Rolls are basically just tiny bread. Which means that, yes, you can technically make a pan of rolls out of any bread dough.

But first, consider the recipe and what type of rolls you're looking to make. If you want soft, fluffy pull-apart rolls (typically baked nestled together in a pan), consider starting with an enriched dough like brioche, milk bread, or challah. If you want crusty, European-style rolls (often baked on sheet trays), start with a leaner dough, such as this pain au levain.

Essentially, the type of bread you start with will determine the type of rolls you make, so plan accordingly.

Turning a bread recipe into rolls is simple: After the dough has had its first rise (otherwise known as its bulk ferment), divide it into small pieces, shape them into rolls, give them a final rise, and bake. The good news is that you don’t need to make any changes to the recipe itself — simply prepare the dough as written and leave it to undergo its first rise.

Once the bread dough has risen, it's time to divide it. Consider: How many rolls do you want, and how large do you want them to be?

Your best bet for even-sized rolls is to grab a calculator and kitchen scale. While you could divide your dough by eye, it’s faster, easier, and more accurate to use the weight measurements, if possible.

For size reference, the pre-bake weight of dinner rolls typically falls between 60g to 80g each. Imagine a 60g roll as the size of a plum when baked, while a baked 80g roll is closer to a Granny Smith apple. Moving up in the ranks are burger buns, which weigh around 100g or so pre-bake.

Here's how much each rolls should weigh before baking:

If you want small-to-medium dinner rolls: 60g to 70g

If you want medium-to-large dinner rolls: 80g to 90g

If you want extra-large dinner rolls or burger buns: 100g to 110g

Let’s say you’re using our Back-of-the-Bag Oatmeal Bread recipe. The total weight of the dough is about 830g. If your first thought is, “I want eight rolls!” you’re going to wind up with eight oat-y burger bun-sized rolls, because 830g divided by eight is just over 100g per roll. That's likely too large if you're looking to make standard dinner rolls.

To ensure you get properly sized rolls, it’s easiest to start by dividing the total weight of the dough by the weight of the size you want your rolls to be, rather than the number of rolls you want. In this case, 830g ÷ 75g = 11 large dinner rolls.

Once divided, it's time to shape the pieces of bread dough. If you’ve never shaped dinner rolls, have no fear! We have you covered, no matter the shape you choose. Basic round rolls? Got it. Fancy shapes? Yep. Braided rolls? You bet. And so much more. Often it helps to see the process in action, especially when it comes to hand positioning when shaping rolls.

For gluten-free breads, scoop the “dough” into a greased muffin pan rather than attempt to shape rolls by hand, since the dough is more like batter. If you're making medium or large gluten-free rolls, check out our Gluten-Free Dinner Rolls recipe for more details.

Small rolls won’t take as long to bake as a loaf would. Most will take around 20 to 30 minutes to bake, depending on their size. You can usually stick with the temperature your original recipe calls for, but 350°F is a safe bet, too.

A final note: Rolls baked close together in "pull-apart" style will usually take a bit longer to bake than they would if they were spaced out on a baking sheet.

And remember, if you make more rolls than you can eat in one sitting, you can always freeze and bake them.

We're diving deep on rolls ahead of Thanksgiving in our latest podcast episode, all about rolls.

#9558. The two-second step to caramelize your pie crust : Just add sugar.

Most pie recipes will instruct you to sprinkle sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar on top of your egg-washed pie crust just before baking, so the coarse sugar can make those edges extra-crunchy and add a bit of glittery sheen. But why stop there — what if the bottom crust got the same treatment too?

That's what our Test Kitchen wondered while developing a new galette recipe for our newest cookbook (coming out next year!). While working on an apricot galette recipe, they tried adding a finishing sugar to the bottom of the dough before baking, and found that it created a crunchy, sugary, caramelized crust that elevated the entire dessert.

As an added bonus, this technique can help ensure a crunchy, well-browned bottom crust;  consider this step another line of defense against a soggy bottom, like baking your pie on a pizza stone or steel or baking pie on the bottom rack of the oven,

You can apply it to any pie (or galette!) recipe while rolling out the dough. Here’s how to do it:

On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough to a 10" to 12" round (aim for the smaller diameter for pie crusts, and larger for galettes). Sprinkle around 1 tablespoon of sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar all over the dough. (It’s important to only use these larger, coarse-grained sugars — we don’t recommend using granulated sugar.) Sprinkle lightly with flour, then continue to roll the dough to reach a 12" to 14" round. Carefully invert the dough round so that the sugared side is on the bottom of the pie pan (to make a single or double crust pie) or parchment paper (to make a galette).

Use this step in classic applications like apple pie where sparkling sugar can cover the entire thing, from top to bottom crust. Or, use it in custard pies like pecan or pumpkin. If you’re going the galette route for Thanksgiving, use it in our Apple Butter Apple Galette or Tiny Apple Tarts for Two. Regardless of the pie you choose, the crust — not the filling! — may be what steals the show.

#9557. This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, said:

“A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”

The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

The memory findings were more complicated.

Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in new information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

Blood samples also showed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

#9556. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

“Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

“Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

“Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor
